-trial C-band 72Gbit/s optical on-off keying
(OOK) system over 18.8km dispersion-uncompensated submarine optical cable in
the South China Sea. Chromatic dispersion (CD) of 18.8km submarine optical
cable causes four spectral nulls on the 36GHz bandwidth of 72Gbit/s OOK signal,
which is the main obstacle for achieving an acceptable bit-error-rate (BER)
performance. Decision feedback equalizer (DFE) is effective to compensate for
the spectral nulls. However, DFE has a serious defect of burst-error
propagation when the burst errors emerge due to the unstable submarine
environment. Weighted DFE (WDFE) can be used to mitigate the burst-error
propagation, but it cannot fully compensate for the spectral nulls because only
a part of feedback symbols is directly decided. Fortunately, maximum likelihood
sequence estimation (MLSE) can be added after the WDFE to simultaneously
compensate for the spectral nulls and burst-error propagation. In addition,
maximum a posteriori probability (MAP) equalizer cannot be used to compensate
for the spectral nulls because of the uncertain channel symbol. However, MAP
equalizer can be added after the WDFE (or MLSE) to refine the equalized output.
In this paper, joint MLSE and MAP equalizer is used to compensate for the spectral
nulls of 72Gbit/s OOK signal and achieve a maximum BER $\leq 7e-3$. Besides,
joint WDFE and MAP equalizer is also used to compensate for the spectral nulls
and give a comparable BER performance to that of joint MLSE and DFE. The
theoretical BER analysis is also given to confirm the feasibility of the joint
equalization design.
  The remaining parts of this paper are organized as follows. In Section II, the
72Gbit/s OOK system model is given. In Section III, joint MLSE and DFE is
proposed to compensate for the spectral nulls of 72Gbit/s OOK signal. In Section
IV, joint WDFE and MAP equalizer is proposed to compensate for the spectral
nulls of 72Gbit/s OOK signal. In Section V, simulation results are given to
verify the effectiveness of the joint equalization designs. Conclusions are
drawn in Section VI.

handling inconsistencies in tables
with missing values (also called nulls) and functional dependencies. Although
the traditional view is that table instances must respect all functional
dependencies imposed on them, it is nevertheless relevant to develop theories
about how to handle instances that violate some dependencies. Regarding missing
values, we make no assumptions on their existence: a missing value exists only
if it is inferred from the functional dependencies of the table.
  We propose a formal framework in which each tuple of a table is associated
with a truth value among the following: true, false, inconsistent or unknown;
and we show that our framework can be used to study important problems such as
consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality measures - to
mention just a few. In this paper, however, we focus mainly on consistent query
answering, a problem that has received considerable attention during the last
decades.
  The main contributions of the paper are the following: (a) we introduce a new
approach to handle inconsistencies in a table with nulls and functional
dependencies, (b) we give algorithms for computing all true, inconsistent and
false tuples, (c) we investigate the relationship between our approach and
Four-valued logic in the context of data merging, and (d) we give a novel
solution to the consistent query answering problem and compare our solution to
that of table repairs.
  We believe that our approaches to handling unknown values and inconsistencies
are quite general and can be used to study other interesting problems, as
mentioned above, and, most importantly, they can be applied to any table
instance, regardless of the underlying data structure. Finally, our experience
in constructing algorithms for computing true, inconsistent and false tuples is
that dynamic programming is a powerful technique to produce efficient
implementations, as we illustrate in our prototype implementation in Java.
  Keywords: functional dependencies, nulls, table merging, unknown values,
consistent query answering, data quality measures.

Tononzintla~2 (Ton~2) using high-resolution near-infrared spectra collected
with the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment II survey
(APOGEE-2), obtained as part of the bulge Cluster APOgee Survey. We investigate
chemical abundances for a variety of species including the light-, odd-Z,
$\alpha$-, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements from high S/N spectra of seven
giant members. The derived mean cluster metallicity is [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$,
with no evidence for an intrinsic metallicity spread. Ton~2 exhibits a typical
$\alpha$-enrichment that follows the trend for high-metallicity Galactic GCs,
similar to that seen in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. We find a significant nitrogen
spread ($>0.87$ dex), and a large fraction of nitrogen-enriched stars that
populate the cluster. Given the relatively high-metallicity of Ton~2, these
nitrogen-enriched stars are well above the typical Galactic levels, indicating
the prevalence of the multiple-population phenomenon in this cluster which also
contains several stars with typical low, first-generation N abundances. We also
identify the presence of [Ce/Fe] $>0$ in five stars, which is one of the most
pronounced [Ce/Fe] trends seen in any GC. Furthermore, we identify three stars
with elevated [Sm/O] that highlight the presence of an antimony clock in these
cluster stars. Lastly, we report the detection of the spectroscopic antimony
line [Sm II] 6283~\AA in two cluster giants, the first such detections in APOGEE
data. Lastly, we discuss the role of antimony in detail, including its status
as a reliable clock in GC stars, the chemical conditions that favour its
production, and its origin in the $s$-process.

has grown to a significant size in the
past years. It makes up for an impressive body of research, which enables a
number of statistical approaches to various aspects in theorem proving, and has
not yet been utilized exhaustively. However, the growing size also poses some
challenges to address: Material becomes increasingly harder to find,
reusability and ease of understanding become more important. This thesis
abstract summarizes my research plans on those topics and touches on some
preliminary results, which indicate that the node in-degree of the dependency
graph of the archive follows a scale-free distribution.
  My plans are divided into three main directions: Through algorithms to
archive entities and their dependencies, I want to investigate methods to
address the reusability issue, including tools for extracting bibliographic
citations from the archive and matching them to the original papers. Secondly,
I want to use the simple yet powerful tooling of Google's PageRank algorithm to
statistically evaluate the importance of files in the archive and discuss the
results philosophically. Lastly, I want to use machine learning to create a
lookup device to enable users to easily find files in the archive that are
most likely to contain results on a given topic.
  Through all of these investigations, I aim to contribute another simple tool
to the archive and in doing so illustrate the connections within it, discuss
approaches to archive growth and highlight the importance of formal reasoning
in a statistical way.
  In a broader sense, my plans further illustrate Isabelle's ability to
facilitate a significant amount of automated and semi-automated proofs within a
single theory, consisting of multiple layers of theories, and how the Isabelle
archive can be viewed as a monolith of proof infrastructure. It demonstrates,
how Isabelle can provide a platform for a large scale experiment in formal
verification, and how it can profit from advanced statistical methods.
  Lastly, my plans showcase Isabelle's ability to seamlessly integrate with
other areas of Computer Science, such as Information Retrieval and Machine
Learning, to borrow powerful algorithmic techniques to solve problems within
the field of theorem proving.
  In summary, through a combination of practical tools and statistical
investigations, I aim to further bridge the gap between the theorem proving and
the wider Computer Science community.

distances follow a general distribution. We consider two main objectives: one
that prioritizes minimal variance and a secondary one that allows for some
variability in order to improve the fields' spatial efficiency. We develop
efficient Markov Chain Monte Carlo procedures for sampling from the two
designs. We show how these designs can be applied to tackle a real-world
problem of allocating resources in a communication network. We perform

the impact of the secondary objective, which we call "redundancy," on the

experiments in high-energy astrophysics is seemingly straightforward, but
reaching high precision of the order of 0.01 in the determination of the
vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) has proven difficult. Wide-field
photometry over a large span of altitudes allows a fast determination of VAOD
independently of the absolute calibration of the system, while providing this
calibration as a useful by-product. Using several years of data taken by the
FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre
Auger Observatory in Argentina and about a year of data taken by a similar
instrument deployed at the planned future Southern site of the Cherenkov
Telescope Array in Chile, we have developed methods to improve the precision of
this measurement technique towards and possibly beyond the 0.01 mark. Detailed
laboratory measurements of the response of the whole system to both the
spectrum and intensity of incoming light have proven indispensable in this
analysis as the usual assumption of linearity of the CCD detectors is not valid
anymore for the conditions of the observations.
  We present the results of this analysis and discuss the prospects for this
method towards next-generation instruments as well as towards using machine
learning techniques to improve the extraction of VAOD from observations.
Finally, we mention how this method can also be used to monitor cosmic ray
intensity.
  Based on the results of this analysis, we conclude that FRAM-like
instruments represent a promising path towards reaching a precision of 0.01 in
the determination of VAOD and beyond, and are worthy of continued and further

D pose of object instances with
convolutional neural network (CNN) has received considerable attention.
Depending on whether intermediate cues are used, the relevant literature can be
roughly divided into two broad categories: direct methods and two stage
pipelines. For the latter, intermediate cues, such as 3D object coordinates,
semantic keypoints, or virtual control points instead of pose parameters are
regressed by CNN in the first stage. Object pose can then be solved by
correspondence constraints constructed with these intermediate cues. In this
paper, we focus on the postprocessing of a two-stage pipeline and propose to
combine two learning concepts for estimating object pose under challenging
scenes: projection grouping on one side, and correspondence learning on the
other. We firstly employ a local patch based method to predict projection
heatmaps which denote the confidence distribution of projection of 3D bounding
box's corners. A projection grouping module is then proposed to remove
redundant local maxima from each layer of heatmaps. Instead of directly feeding
2D-3D correspondences to the perspective-n-point (PnP) algorithm, multiple
correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and its corresponding
neighborhood and ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Finally,
correspondences with higher confidence are selected to determine object pose.
Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that the proposed
framework outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in terms of both
accuracy and efficiency.

edge-weighted, potentially directed, graphs over the same set of nodes with

node in a given layer is based on the weighted sum of the importance of

assume that the adjacency relationship and the importance of adjacent nodes may

mutually distrustful subsystems.

security-critical programs, we show that this machine significantly reduces the
required trust compared to mainstream TEEs while achieving decent performance.
For normal programs, performance is similar to a legacy machine.

has the potential to significantly lower security costs for smartphone owners
and, by extension, anyone who needs to run security-critical programs on an
untrusted platform.

problems can be formulated as functional optimization problems with
differential equality and inequality constraints. Since these problems are
infinite-dimensional and often do not have a known analytical solution, one has
to resort to numerical methods to compute an approximate solution. This paper
uses a unifying notation to outline some of the techniques used in the
transcription step of simultaneous direct methods (which
discretize-then-optimize) for solving continuous-time dynamic optimization
problems. We focus on collocation, integrated residual and Runge-Kutta schemes.
These transcription methods are then applied to a simulation case study to
answer a question that arose during the COVID-19 pandemic, namely: If there are
not enough ventilators, is it possible to ventilate more than one patient on a
single ventilator? The results suggest that it is possible, in principle, to
estimate individual patient parameters sufficiently accurately, using a
relatively small number of flow rate measurements, to enable this scenario. We
also provide a open source Python code that implements the transcription
techniques and simulates the proposed ventilating-two-patients-on-one-ventilator
scheme.
  Which transcription scheme is best? There is not a definitive answer to this
question, as the choice of transcription scheme will depend on the specific
problem that one is trying to solve, namely: is it a smooth problem or a
nonsmooth optimization problem? Are the constraints differentiable or
nondifferentiable? etc. In any case, it is useful to have several transcription
schemes available, so that one can experiment with different formulations of
the problem. For example, one can use a collocation scheme to solve a
nonsmooth optimization problem, by transcribing it into a smooth optimization
problem, and then using a nonlinear program solver to solve the transcribed
problem. This can be very useful, indeed, for solving some of the optimal
control problems that arise in mechanical engineering applications. In
contrast, the system identification problems that we consider in this paper have
smooth constraints, and thus one can use a higher-order transcription scheme,

ophageal tumor in CT images is known
to be very challenging. This is due to the low contrast between the tumor and
adjacent tissues, the anatomical variation of the esophagus, as well as the
occasional presence of foreign bodies (e.g. feeding tubes). Physicians
therefore usually exploit additional knowledge such as endoscopic findings,
clinical history, additional imaging modalities like PET scans. Achieving his
additional information is time-consuming, while the results are error-prone and
might lead to non-deterministic results. In this paper we aim to investigate if
and to what extent a simplified clinical workflow based on CT alone, allows one
to automatically segment the esophageal tumor with sufficient quality. For this
purpose, we present a fully automatic end-to-end esophageal tumor segmentation
method based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The proposed network,
called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), leverages spatial and channel
attention gates in each dense block to selectively concentrate on determinant
feature maps and regions. Dilated convolutional layers are used to manage GPU
memory and increase the network receptive field. We collected a dataset of 792
scans from 288 distinct patients including varying anatomies with \mbox{air
pockets}, feeding tubes and proximal tumors. Repeatability and reproducibility
studies were conducted for three distinct CT scans each from 50 distinct
patients. We also investigated the segmentor robustness to varying image
quality. Our method was compared against six state-of-the-art automatic
segmentation methods. It successfully segmented the esophageal tumor with a
mean score of 0.75 against a manual score of 0.79. A statistically highly
significant agreement was found between manual and automatic segmentations
(Cohen's $\omega$ = 0.30). The repeated segmentations for each of the 50
repeatability and reproducibility studies had a mean DICE score of 0.78 $\pm$
0.18, indicating high repeatability. The mean DICE score for segmentations
performed by two human annotators had a mean of 0.79 $\pm$ 0.14, while the
mean DICE score for automatic segmentations had a mean of 0.75 $\pm$ 0.14,
indicating a high agreement with human annotators and a counter-intuitive
improvement (about 3%)

one of core knowledge
extraction techniques, named entity recognition (NER) is widely used to extract
information from texts for downstream tasks. Nested NER is a branch of NER in
which the named entities (NEs) are nested with each other. However, most of the
previous studies on nested NER usually apply linear structure to model the
nested NEs which are actually accommodated in a hierarchical structure. Thus in
order to address this mismatch, this work models the full nested NEs in a
sentence as a holistic structure, then we propose a holistic structure parsing
algorithm to disclose the entire NEs once for all. Besides, there is no
research on applying corpus-level information to NER currently. To make up for
the loss of this information, we introduce Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI)
and other frequency features from corpus-aware statistics for even better
performance by holistic modeling from sentence-level to corpus-level.
Experiments show that our model yields promising results on widely-used
benchmarks which approach or even achieve state-of-the-art. Further empirical
studies show that our proposed corpus-aware features can substantially improve
NER domain adaptation, which demonstrates the surprising advantage of our
proposed corpus-level holistic structure modeling.

introduce Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI) and other frequency features from
corpus-aware statistics for even better performance by holistic modeling from
sentence-level to corpus-level.

preprocessing steps and tested the pipeline with and without them. We further

of distribution systems after disruptions in transportation and power networks.
To investigate this issue, we propose a framework of network-based multi-agent
optimization problems with equilibrium constraints (N-MOPEC) to consider the
decentralized decision making of stakeholders in transportation and energy systems.
However, solving this problem is computationally challenging due to its
non-convexity and high dimensionality. To address this issue, we develop an
efficient computational algorithm to solve the high-dimensional non-convex
problem. In particular, we use the linearization technique to represent the
non-convex subproblems equivalently as convex second-order cone programming
problems. We also use decentralization techniques -- exact convex
reformulation and Lagrangian decomposition -- to solve the global optimization
problem through coordinating the local optimization problems of individual
stakeholders. Numerical studies are conducted to illustrate the effectiveness
of our modeling and computational approach and to draw policy insights. The
proposed modeling and computational strategies provide a solid foundation for the
future study of power system resilience with private EVs in coupled
transportation and power networks.

their lower bandwidth and higher latency. When used in this Memory (or cached)
mode, Optane DC memory has little impact on applications with small memory
footprints. Applications with larger memory footprints may experience some
slow-down relative to DRAM, but are now able to keep much more data in memory.
When used under a file system, Optane DC PMMs can result in significant
performance gains, especially when the file system is optimized to use the
load/store interface of the Optane DC PMM and the application uses many small,

can improve the performance of deduplication, checksum updates, and small

future memory scratchpads may be designed to exploit the high capacity of

creation and control
of high-performance solid-state telecom photon-spin interfaces. T radiation
damage centres in silicon provide a promising photon-spin interface due to
their narrow O-band optical transition near 1326 nm and long-lived electron and
nuclear spin lifetimes. To date, these defect centres have only been studied as
ensembles in bulk silicon. Here, we demonstrate the reliable creation of high
concentration T centre ensembles in the 220 nm device layer of
silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers by ion implantation and subsequent annealing.
We then develop a method that uses spin-dependent optical transitions to
benchmark the characteristic optical spectral diffusion within these T centre
ensembles. Using this new technique, we show that with minimal optimization to
the fabrication process high densities of implanted T centres localized
$\lesssim$100 nm from an interface display ~1 GHz characteristic levels of
total spectral diffusion.
  Finally, we show that by implementing sophisticated magnetic field filtering
that the single-photon detectors attached to these T centre ensembles can
achieve ~10% absolute detection efficiency and ~1 ns timing resolution. Our
results demonstrate that SOI T centre ensembles are capable of withstanding the
device fabrication processes and integration conditions necessary for global
quantum networking applications.

efficient collection protocol for Wireless Sensor Networks. The former is the
Bidirectional Link Quality Estimation, which allows nodes to easily and quickly
compute the quality of a link between a pair of nodes. The latter, Hierarchical
Range Sectoring, organizes sensors in different sectors based on their location
within the network. Based on this organization, nodes from each sector are
coordinated to transmit in specific periods of time to reduce the hidden
terminal problem. To evaluate these two mechanisms, a protocol called HBCP
(Hierarchical-Based Collection Protocol), that implements both mechanisms, has
been implemented in TinyOS 2.1, and evaluated in a testbed using TelosB motes.
The results show that the HBCP protocol is able to achieve a very high
reliability, especially in large networks and in scenarios with bottlenecks.
Although the computation of the link quality is simple and fast, we can observe
that the contribution of Hierarchical Range Sectoring to the overall reliability
is more important than the contribution of the Bidirectional Link Quality
Estimation. Regarding energy consumption, we can see that the HBCP protocol is
able to save up to 27% of energy consumption when compared to a traditional
collection protocol.
  In this article, we present a survey of techniques for clustering Wireless
Sensor Networks (WSNs). We present partitioning techniques, which are simple to
implement, but static and inflexible. We also present hierarchical techniques,
which are more flexible, but harder to implement. Beyond that, we present
quality of service (QoS) techniques, which aim to improve the network and system
performance, but with a higher computational cost. In addition, we present
dynamic clustering techniques, which are able to adapt to changes in the network
and to optimize resource consumption. Finally, we present some applications of
WSNs and examples of their usage in different areas.
  In this article, we present a survey of techniques for range estimation in
Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs). We present MAC protocols to enable devices to
determine each other's distances, which can be used to improve the accuracy of
a network location algorithms. We also present location algorithms to estimate
the geographic location of the nodes in the network and also analyze techniques
to calculate the energy efficiency of different protocols and algorithms. At the
end, we present some applications of the range estimation area and examples of
their usage in different scenarios.

action are encoded in the representation learned by deep object detectors for

without any human-specific learning. Our results, unlike the common
observations that deep learners are poor at distinguishing visually similar

transplantation (KT). The increasing shortage of kidney donors has driven the
development of desensitization techniques to overcome this immunological
challenge. Compared with compatible KT, patients undergoing incompatible KTs
are more likely to experience rejection, infection, malignancy, and graft loss.
We study the optimal acceptance of possibly incompatible kidneys for individual
end-stage kidney disease patients. To capture the effect of incompatibility, we
propose a Markov Decision Process (MDP) model that explicitly includes
compatibility as a state variable. The resulting higher-dimensional model makes
it more challenging to analyze, but under suitable conditions, we derive
structural properties including control limit-type optimal policies that are
easy to compute and implement. Numerical examples illustrate the behavior of
the optimal policy under different mismatch levels and highlight the importance
of explicitly incorporating the incompatibility level into the acceptance
decision when desensitization therapy is an option.
  We also consider a two-parameter model with mismatch level and panel reactive
antibody (PRA) level, and show that the optimal policy is a combination of two
thresholds: a lower threshold for the PRA level and an upper threshold for the
mismatch level. This model is also solvable using our structural properties
methodology. Finally, in a three-parameter model with mismatch level, PRA
level, and donor age, we use our structural properties to derive a feasible
suboptimal policy that is easy to compute and implement, and is tailored to
practice. Numerical examples illustrate the suboptimal policy's performance
and sensitivity to parameter changes. Again, the structure of the problem
allows for a feasible suboptimal policy that is simple to compute and
implement, yet provides near-optimal performance.

state of incompatibility influences not only the current acceptance decision
but also the future expected utility and optimal action. This is because
accepting a possibly incompatible kidney may increase the risk of rejection,
which in turn increases the PRA level, and thus the risk of rejecting a
future compatible kidney.

high dimensions. This broad class of copulas is partially defined through
decomposition copulas, which are mappings that slice a copula into its marginal
distributions. In this article, we introduce orthogonal decomposition copulas
that are intuitive definitions of copulas for high-dimensional data. These
implicit copulas are parameterized by an orthogonal matrix and a baseline
copula. They ensure that the marginal dependencies conform to the elliptical
distributions, which is often an adequate assumption in financial engineering
and risk management. The elegant structure of orthogonal decomposition copulas
allows for fast evaluation times even in high dimensions. We provide a
comprehensive study of this new family of copulas, including methods for
generating random variables, inference via maximum likelihood, and popular
risk measures such as Value-at-Risk and expected short fall. A benchmark study
on Frechet scores indicates that elliptical copulas, including the orthogonal
decomposition copulas, outperform other implicit copulas in terms of diversity
and adaptability. We also propose a novel algorithm for forecasting orthogonal
decomposition copulas and show its effectiveness in a forecasting study of
stock returns and wind speeds.

model, especially when it is equipped with the Skip-gram learning scheme. Our
goal is to explain how embeddings, that are now widely used in NLP (Natural
Language Processing), are influenced by the distribution of terms in the
documents of the considered corpus. We use a mathematical formulation to shed
light on how the decision to use such a model makes implicit assumptions on the
structure of the language. We show how Markovian assumptions, that we discuss,
lead to a very clear theoretical understanding of the formation of embeddings,
and in particular the way it captures what we call frequentist synonyms. These
assumptions allow to produce generative models and to conduct an explicit
analysis of the loss function commonly used by these NLP techniques. Moreover,
we produce synthetic corpora with different levels of structure and show
empirically how the word2vec algorithm succeed, or not, to learn them. It leads
us to empirically assess the capability of such models to capture structures on
a corpus of around 42 millions of financial News covering 12 years. That for,
we rely on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists largely used on financial
texts and we show that embeddings are exposed to mixing terms with opposite
polarity, because of the way they can treat antonyms as frequentist synonyms.
Beside we study the non-stationarity of such a model and the role of
overfitting, by looking at the probability of co-occurrence produced at
different training parameter settings. This work complements the analysis
initiated by Taylor et al. (2018) on the monolingual extension of the model and
shows empirically that embeddings are above all influenced by the structure of
a single language, rather than any cross-lingual structure.

linguistics rely on unary modalities to allow for the controlled application of
structural rules affecting word order and phrase structure. These controlled
structural operations give rise to derivational ambiguities that are missed by
the original Lambek Calculus or its pregroup simplification. Proposals for
compositional interpretation of extended Lambek Calculus in the compact closed
category of FVect and linear maps have been made, but in these proposals the
syntax-semantics mapping ignores the control modalities, effectively
restricting their role to the syntax. Our aim is to turn the modalities into
first-class citizens of the vectorial interpretation. Building on the
directional density matrix semantics, we extend the interpretation of the type
system with an extra spin density matrix space. The interpretation of proofs
then results in ambiguous derivations being tensored with orthogonal spin
states. Our method introduces a way of simultaneously representing co-existing
interpretations of ambiguous utterances, and provides a uniform framework for
the integration of lexical and derivational ambiguity.
  We achieve this extension by adding a second matrix space to the matrix
interpretation of proofs. The spin representation is motivated by the
Danish language which makes extensive use of word order and phrase structure
modifications in comparison to other Germanic languages. We show how our method
models the co-existence of subject and non-subject word order in Danish as
represented in a recent pregroup derivation bank for Danish. Our approach allows
for the integration of data-driven derivation banks with a rich type system
capable of capturing ambiguities arising from structural rules. Finally, our
method provides a way of computing all possible orderings of ambiguous phrases
and thus derives the set of derivations from a single "fuzzy" input derivation.
This is particularly useful for the integration of lexical and derivational
ambiguity in a cross-linguistic setting.

rationalizable behavior, where players learn to avoid iteratively dominated
actions. However, even in the basic setting of multiplayer general-sum games,
existing algorithms require a number of samples exponential in the number of
players to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper
develops the first line of efficient algorithms for learning rationalizable
Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) whose sample
complexities are polynomial in all problem parameters including the number of
players. To achieve this result, we also develop a new efficient algorithm for
the simpler task of finding one rationalizable action profile (not necessarily
an equilibrium), whose sample complexity substantially improves over the best
existing results of Wu et al. (2021). Our algorithms incorporate several novel
techniques to guarantee rationalizability and no (swap-)regret simultaneously,
including a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which
may be of independent interest. We complement our results with a sample
complexity lower bound showing the sharpness of our guarantees.

$\to$ infective $\to$ recovered) epidemic model
defined on a social network is analysed. The underlying social network is
described by an Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi random graph but, during the course of the
epidemic, susceptible individuals connected to infectious neighbours may drop
or rewire such connections. Large population limits of the model are derived
giving both convergence results for the early branching process-like behaviour,
and, assuming a major outbreak, the main phase of the epidemic process which
converges to a deterministic model that is equivalent to a certain pair
approximation model. Law of large numbers results are also obtained for the
final size (i.e. total number of individuals infected) of a major outbreak. Two
results stand out (valid for a range of parameter set-ups): (i) the limiting
final fraction infected may be discontinuous in the infection rate $\lambda$ at
its threshold $\lambda_c$ (thus making a discrete jump from $0$ to a strictly
positive number) and (ii) for the situation when rewiring is necessarily to
uninfected individuals, if it is discontinuous, the limiting final fraction
infected jumps from $0$ to $1$ as $\lambda$ passes through $\lambda_c$.
Nonetheless, if rewiring is not necessarily to uninfected individuals, then if
discontinuous, the limiting final fraction infected jumps from $0$ to a strictly
positive number, but which can be arbitrarily close to $0$ (and similarly for
the susceptible fraction).
  We also consider the additional effect of a vaccine taking, independent of
infection, in some individuals. This gives two further results for the case when
rewiring is necessarily to uninfected individuals: (iii) the limiting equilibrium
proportion of the population with vaccine may be zero, or, for certain
parameter ranges, strictly positive; (iv) if a sufficient percentage of the
population receive the vaccine then the epidemic will not occur (or at least
no significant outbreak) as the basic reproduction number $R_0$ of the epidemic
is assumed to be at least nominally less than or equal to $1$.
  Finally, we consider the effect of both a vaccine and of rewiring, for a new
outbreak of the epidemic occurring in a population which had previously been
infected but from which all individuals had recovered and were now immune.

dynamically impact the output trajectories, it is desirable to effectively
leverage the information from historical samples for better policy training.
Most of existing methods tend to revisit the problematic scenarios by
re-tracing the old samples, which is inefficient. Instead, we propose to use the
deep kernel extrapolation to utilize the information from all the samples,
irrespective of whether the new states have been visited before. We derive the
specificive policy function for the deep process kernel and estimate the
expectation by weighted nearest neighbors. Importantly, the complexity of each
sampling step is roughly $O(n)$. We show that our approach guarantees
approximately the same cumulative reward as the ideal adapter with infinite
memory. Experiments demonstrate that our method is effective and efficient
especially when the underlying dynamics are complex and the adaptation learning
is difficult.

quark polarisation, in $t$-channel single top quark production is presented. It
is based on a sample of pp collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of 8 TeV
corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 19.7 $\mathrm{fb^{-1}}$. A
high-purity sample of $t$-channel single top quark events with an isolated muon
is selected. Signal and background components are estimated using a fit to
data. A differential cross section measurement, corrected for detector effects,
of an angular observable sensitive to the top quark polarisation is performed.
The differential distribution is used to extract a top quark spin asymmetry of
$0.26 \pm 0.03 \textrm{(stat)} \pm 0.10 \textrm{(syst)}$, which is compatible
with a p-value of $4.6\%$ with the standard model prediction of 0.44. An
alternative measurement, where the angular observable depends on the $s$-channel
process, yields a consistent result. The present result can be interpreted
as evidence for the presence of polarised strangeness in the proton. Performed
for the first time, this measurement opens a new approach to determining the

spin-glass, suggesting a close proximity to a spin-glass state.

thickness-dependent behavior, with the fast relaxing component being the
dominant in the thinnest and thickest samples, while the metallic component is
predominant in between. This field dependence is qualitatively consistent
with a field-induced separation of two components with different $T$-dependencies
and is discussed in more detail elsewhere.

samples are those with the greatest LaNiO$_3$ disorder, consistent with
magnetic fluctuations mediated by spin-dependent charge ordering.

material and model them with a simple mean field model in which the metallic
and fast relaxing components are identified with the coupled ferromagnetic and
antiferromagnetic spins of the C-type charge and magnetic ordering.

control system, and publishing platform. Its potential uses are open-ended -
its processing is controlled by makefiles that are straightforward to customize

other purposes.

social practices in the research community. It seeks to address some of the
disadvantages of the current state of research software development, and to
assist with the goal of increasing the transparency and reproducibility of
research. It could be useful to any team of collaborators who need to work on
interconnected files of any type, and particularly to teams of researchers who
need to work on software projects or documents with complex dependencies.

walk in a different lattice geometry, leading to a peculiar dynamics
characterized by more than one time scale. The latter is general for any
lattice geometry, but it is especially relevant in triangular and diamond

respectively. As a result, dimers experience partial quasi-localization due to
an effective flat band, and may move slower than longer clusters. This
surprising link between anomalously slow quantum walk dynamics in these models
and flat-band physics may be readily observed in experiments with lanthanide
atoms.

momentum. This is manifested in observed non-Flat-Band-Soliton dynamics, which
forms a peculiar rotating motion along the flat band, and also in a phenomenon
of "spin-momentum trapping," which may be observed in experiments with lanthanide
atoms. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the dynamics of
inter-site interactions in quantum gases.

may be scaled down by a factor of more than $10^4$ and still bind nearest
neighbors. This makes lanthanide-based implementations particularly promising
for observing phenomena of inter-site cluster dynamics in two-dimensional
lattices.

molecules and crystals. We show that the circular motion of ions introduces
inertial effects on electrons. In analogy to the classical Coriolis and
centrifugal forces, these effects are the spin-rotation coupling, the
centrifugal field coupling, the centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and the
centrifugal redshift. Depending on the phonon decay, these effects persist for
various picoseconds after excitation. Potential boosting of the effects would
make it a promising platform for vibration-based control of localized quantum
states or chemical reaction barriers.
  From THz phonon excitation in rare-earth fluorides, we identify the time
scales on which the circular motion develops and persists. We find that the
centrifugal field coupling and the centrifugal redshift scale with phonon
frequency and range from a few kHz to a few MHz, while the spin-rotation
coupling and the centrifugal spin-orbit coupling scale with the electron
orbital radius and range from a few MHz to a few GHz. Furthermore, we show
that one-dimensional circular motion introduces only spin-rotation coupling and
centrifugal field coupling, while the centrifugal redshift and centrifugal
spin-orbit coupling are two-dimensional phenomena.
  To further explore the physics, we use a classical model to follow the
evolution of ions and electrons, describe the creation of vacuum pairs
resulting in persistent electric current, and show that a rotating superlattice
may induce persistent magnetization. Additionally, we show that the centrifugal
field coupling can be used for vibration-controlled switching of an artificial
atomic-level diode and that the centrifugal redshift can be used for
vibration-controlled spectral shifting of an artificial atomic-level emitter.
Finally, we report that the centrifugal effects may be explored in various
phonon-excitable systems.

contributions to improving diversity in dialogue generation. First, we propose
a novel metric which uses Natural Language Inference (NLI) to measure the
semantic diversity of a set of model responses for a conversation. We evaluate
this metric using an established framework (Tevet and Berant, 2021) and find

model's confidence achieves state-of-the-art results. Second, we demonstrate
how to iteratively improve the semantic diversity of a sampled set of responses
via a new generation procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which

conversations that cover various aspects of the topic. However, they often
generate monotonous responses that indicate limited understanding of the topic
terms. This paper proposes a new method called Diversity Threshold Generation
for generating diverse, interesting responses that cover the semantic scope
of the conversation. Our method uses the conversational context and the
dictionary of the domain to guide the search space of the generation model.

dictionary and generates diverse responses that cover all the terms. Our best
model achieves an average 137% increase in NLI Diversity compared to baseline

classes and an imbalance due to incremental learning is added to the initial
dataset imbalance. A score prediction bias in favor of new classes is
introduced, we measure it and evaluate that it translates a practical
performance gap between old and new classes. We propose a new loss function,
called Score Decomposition Loss, to break this bias and evaluate it on four
incremental learning datasets with imbalanced classes. It outperforms the
state of the art by 5% mean accuracy and reduces the novelties gap to the
state of the art within 3 incremental states.
  Our code is available at https://github.com/AymanFathi/Score-Decomposition-Loss.
## Conclusion
In this work, we studied the problem of incremental learning from imbalanced
datasets. We measured and evaluated the score prediction bias of existing
algorithms, we proposed a new loss function called Score Decomposition Loss to
break it and compare it to the state of the art. SD-Loss is a straightforward
modification to existing algorithms and it has been effective across different
datasets and architectures. It is a practical solution to the class imbalance
problem of incremental learning from non-stationary datasets.
## Reproducibility
To ensure reproducibility, we provide the hyperparameters settings in the
code. Also, we provide the dataset download scripts to ensure that the
datasets are downloaded in the same way in different runs.

Fields like graph computer, graphs theory, and machine learning use matrices
very often to solve their own problems. The most often matrix operation is the
multiplication. It may be time-consuming if the matrices to be multiplied are
large. To overcome this issue, the distributed computing is used. In
particular, the Hadamard parallel matrix multiplication is one of the most
popular algorithms in this area. It recursively splits the multiplication into
smaller sub-problems for each processor. It is scalable and efficient. However,
it is static - it does not adapt to the number of processors and their
performance. This is not acceptable in many practical scenarios. Another
issue, the Hadamard scheme does not suit the modern computer clusters that much.
It does not utilize the block matrix feature of the modern computers very much.
This is why we propose a new approach to the Hadamard scheme - it is dynamic,
adapts to the number of processors and their performance, and utilizes the
feature of block matrices in computers of the cluster type. The results of our
experiments are very promising - they indicate that our approach may be up to
12 times faster than the Hadamard scheme, and it has good scalability. It can
effectively utilize up to 256 processors. The experimental evidence
demonstrates that our algorithm can effectively utilize the performance
difference between the processors. We conduct our experiments on two clusters,
one on the computers with the almost equal performance, and the other with
significant performance difference between the computers. We also discuss some
interesting mathematical facts revealed during the development and
experimentation of our algorithm.
  From the mathematical point of view, the paper reveals some interesting
properties of the matrix multiplication, in particular, how to represent the
three-dimensional iteration space of the Hadamard scheme as a set of two-dimensional matrices and how to effectively utilize the block matrix feature of the computers of the cluster type. These considerations lead to the following generic recommendations how to effectively implement the Hadamard scheme: (1) represent the iteration space as a set of two-dimensional matrices; (2) utilize the feature of the block matrix operation support in the computers of the cluster type; and (3) sort the matrices in a way that the communication overhead is minimized. These considerations are generic and applicable to any matrix multiplication algorithm utilizing the scheme-like approach, including the column-wise matrix multiplication (also known as the pinwheel scheme), the fuzzy matrix multiplication, and all other similar

distribution independent of training data, it requires sufficient large number

the number of feature dimensions is necessary to effectively scale to large
datasets. In this paper, we propose a kernel approximation method in a data
dependent way, coined as Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF) for reducing the

experiments on the COCO benchmark validate the soundness of our analysis and

attacks on networks, is focused on measuring some macro parameters related to
an entire attack, such as the critical probability of a percolation occurrence

network - the giant component, but not considering the attack on a micro
perspective, which is the analysis of the node removals, during an attack,
themselves, their characteristics and results. In this paper we present and
apply the last method of focusing on the micro scale of an attack. Based on the
theory of percolation in networks, we analyze the phenomenon of an avalanche
results due to a single node removal from a network, that is a state in which a
removal of one node belongs to the network's giant component causes other nodes
to be also disconnected from it, which is a much greater contribution to the
fragmentation (immunization) of the network than only the single original node
removal itself. Specifically, we focus ourselves on the parameter of the size
of an avalanche, which is the number of nodes that are disconnected from the
giant component due to a single node removal. Relating to a sharp cutoff
phenomenon, we also established thresholds for the distribution of the
parameters of interest, which are the avalanche size and the original node
degree, at the point of the maximum of the corresponding cumulative distribution
functions. We performed our analysis on four social networks, which are
sufficiently large to present a sharp cutoff phenomenon in their underlying
graph percolation model, and thus sufficient to test our main point regarding
the sharp cutoff of the avalanche size distribution. Our results are consistent

cutoff phenomenon is even enhanced in larger networks, from the viewpoint of

conclude that the social aspect of the links between the nodes, which is

the percolation phenomenon in the network, which in turn implies an important
range of application of the percolation theory

satisfy a desired point symmetry but are built from the combination of
lower-symmetry primitive cells. We define as structural prototypes the smallest
of these that are both energetically and dynamically stable. Remarkably, two
40-atom prototypes can be identified for paraelectric BaTiO$_3$; these are also
common to many other $AB$O$_3$ perovskites. These prototypes can offer
structural models of paraelectric phases that can be used for the computational
engineering of functional materials. Last, we show that the emergence of

controlled by the equilibrium volume, in turn dictated by the filler A cation.
This indicates that the intrinsic character of the Ti off-centerings is real,
and not an artifact of any particular crystallographic condition.

for exploring the competing orders that B-cation off-centerings can initiate,

effectively prevents 34% of runtime type errors, but also imposes 2.5x overhead

iOCR. iOCR was developed with a spell correction algorithm to fix errors
introduced by conventional OCR for vote tabulation. The results found that the
iOCR system outperforms conventional OCR techniques.
  From a computer science perspective, the iOCR system can be seen as a
method to improve the performance of OCR techniques (i.e., text recognition)
on unnatural text such as hand-written ballots. From a statistical
perspective, this can be viewed as a method to adjust estimates to obtain
attained population parameters (i.e., the mean vector of vote tabulation),
which are more relevant to election outcomes.
  In the United States, federal law mandates that paper trails be produced
for all elections so that votes can be audited. Paper trails are usually
produced by using scanners and OCR techniques on ballot images to
automatically obtain vote counts. However, as demonstrated in several
real-world experiments, conventional OCR techniques can introduce
significant errors rates (e.g., 7%) for hand-written ballots. These errors
can lead to incorrect attainted population parameters, and subsequently
alterate election outcomes that could impact confidence in democratic
institutions. This paper describes an Informed OCR or iOCR system developed to
address this issue. The iOCR system first produces an uncorrected vote count
using conventional OCR techniques and then adjusts the result using a spell
correction algorithm. Experiments were conducted on 2000 hand-written
mock-up ballots (also called "mock ballots"). The results found that the iOCR
system outperforms conventional OCR techniques. For example, the error rate

of firming in low-carbon grids. A
common concern raised from ex-post assessments is that storage resources can
fail to respond to strong price signals during times of scarcity. While
commonly attributed to forecast error or failures in operations, we posit that
this behavior can be explained from the perspective of risk-averse scheduling.
Using a stochastic self-scheduling framework and real-world data harvested from
the Australian National Electricity Market, we demonstrate that risk-averse
storage resources tend to have a myopic operational perspective, that is, they
typically engage in near-term price arbitrage and chase only few extreme price
spikes and troughs, thus remaining idle in several time periods with markedly
high and low prices. This has important policy implications given the
non-transparency of unit risk aversion and apparent risk in intervention
decision-making.
  We further show that even though risk aversion leads to a marginal unit
forecast error, it does not affect risk premium payments. Moreover, it does not
induce herding behavior among storage resources nor does it affect market
clearing prices. Finally, calculating the social welfare of each market trading
session, we demonstrate that risk aversion can lead to a loss of potential
welfare for the grid.
  Our findings are critical for ex-ante scheduling and risk management of
storage resources, and highlight the importance of addressing the implications
of risk aversion in the context of ex-post price determination.
  In doing so, we provide an Australia-specific but generally applicable insight
into the role of storage in ensuring reliability of supply in low-carbon grids.
We conclude that advanced risk aversion models remain prone to interpretations
and over-parametrization, and that simple utility function specifications can
provide insightful results in the context of stochastic scheduling.
  We also conclude that further research is needed to address the impact of
risk aversion in the context of multi-period scheduling, particularly, towards
simulating entire dispatch trajectories and accounting for unit replacement and
new entrants in the market.
  Finally, we recommend that National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) and
Independent System Operators (ISOs) revisit their scheduling models towards
accounting for the implications of risk aversion in the context of storage
resources.
  We hope this work contributes towards re-examining storage's role in ensuring
reliability of supply and towards contributing to more sustainable future
markets.

  Distributed estimation in sensor networks is known to suffer from the
impracticality of direct connection to the destination. In particular, when
interference is present on the communication links, the use of intermediate
relays is necessary to achieve a satisfactory level of performance. This is
where cooperative diversity comes into play. However, the use of cooperative
diversity schemes implies delay due to the necessary number of transmissions.
To address this issue, we propose a novel non-cooperative diversity scheme
which eliminates the need for direct link transmission and intermediate relays.
The proposed scheme achieves diversity gain by exploiting the reflected versions
of the origin sensor's measurement at the destination. We investigate the
performance of the proposed scheme in terms of mean squared error (MSE) bound,
and we show that the diversity gain is determined by the reflectivity of the
environment plus the number of paths between the sensor and the destination. We
show that the proposed scheme is superior in practical scenarios such as
urban areas, especially when the number of scattering is large. In addition, we
show that the proposed scheme is better than the direct transmission when the
number of scattering is large compared to the number of diversity links. We
verify the theoretical results with Monte-Carlo simulations.

labeling strategies exist, making the choice difficult. We propose a novel
strategy, which is based on both a checker agent that calculates a trust score
of each instance and a general framework for building a labeling strategy. We
evaluate this strategy on the MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets, with and without
geometric data augmentation and retraining using transfer learning. We show that
it outperforms other labeling strategies in terms of accuracy and trust score,
and we provide a check-list of a good labeling strategy.

proposed private GNN architectures, but the necessary foundation work, such as

simulating the otherwise difficult-to-compute dynamics of quantum many-body
systems. In this work we derive, within the positive-P phase-space formalism, a
new stochastic hydrodynamic method for the description of interacting Bose
gases. It goes beyond existing hydrodynamic approaches, such as superfluid
hydrodynamics or generalized hydrodynamics, in its capacity to simulate the
full quantum dynamics of these systems: it possesses the ability to compute
non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena.
Using this description, we derive a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme
which is able to simulate such non-equilibrium situations for longer times than
the full positive-P approach, at the expense of approximating the treatment of
quantum fluctuations, and show that this linearized scheme can be directly
connected with existing Bogoliubov approaches. Furthermore, we go on to
demonstrate the usefulness and advantages of this formalism by exploring the
correlations that arise in a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its
predictions to other established quantum many-body approaches.
  We also use this hydrodynamic description to investigate the quantum
fluctuations in rotating superfluids. In particular, we observe the emergence
of vortices in the O(2) invariant planar O(N)-rotating superfluid that can
be described as localized solitons for large rotational velocities. These
vortices possess characteristics which are different to those in rotating
superfluids with O(3) symmetry, such as the incompressible hydrodynamic description
of planar rotating superfluids, which is not valid for the vortex states. We
also show that these vortices can be created by quantum pair creation of
superfluid particles and investigate the correlation functions which are
associated with the creation of these vortices.

previously developed hydrodynamic and Bogoliubov approaches, identify its
ingredients and emphasize its usefulness for simulating the full quantum

observed in the edge plasma of the JET tokamak. Although PTMs are well
documented, little is known about the mechanisms which produce these
structures. In the case of the PTM, an ELM-postcursor, its genesis is usually
explained by ergodisation of the magnetic field due to edge localized modes and
the appearance of a seed magnetic island which evolves into a PTM later. In
this study we try to invoke a creation mechanism based on the concepts and
observations in edge plasma turbulence. An interesting aspect of plasma
turbulence is the occurrence of coherent, long-lived structures in the
scrape-off-layer (SOL). These localized and magnetic-field-aligned regions with
higher or lower plasma densities are called blobs and holes. Measurements show
that these filaments carry parallel currents. We thus here interpret
ELM-filaments as massive blobs and the interspace between these filaments as
holes. We demonstrate that a forward-modelled closed current filament on a q=3
surface produces similar magnetic fluctuations as measured by the JET in-vessel
magnetic pickup coils if a PTM is present. From that we deduce that if a hole
is captured on a q=3 surface after an ELM-crash, a PTM equivalent signature is
generated. If the ELM-filament itself is captured on a q=3 surface, the
filtration effect of the q-only magnetic field leads to a strong magnification
of the filaments' magnetic fluctuations in the toroidal direction, which
explains the broadened signatures observed. If the ELM-filament is not
captured, the typical narrow signature is produced by the interacting current
filament and the q-only magnetic field.
  The paper demonstrates that the two creation mechanisms of PTMs; the
ergodisation of the magnetic field and the ELM-induced compression of a magnetic
island, as well as the movement and the interaction of the ELM-filaments play
an important role in the dynamics of PTMs. The study highlights the similarities
between the concepts of plasma turbulence in the SOL and the dynamics of the
magnetic islands.

the interaction of the filaments and the q-only magnetic field as well as a
comparison with more extensive measurements including the fast camera films and
the edge plasma density measurements from the safety monitoring system.

considerable progress in this area in the past years, measuring and comparing
the effectiveness of fuzzers is still an open research question. In software
testing, the gold standard for evaluating test quality is mutation analysis,
assessing the ability of a test to detect synthetic bugs; if a set of tests
fails to detect such mutations, it is incomplete with respect to that set.
Mutation analysis subsumes various coverage measures and has recently been
applied to fuzzing. However, its applications are still few, mainly due to the
high cost of computing mutations in experimental settings. We propose Mutator,
a novel, efficient mutator based on binary translation that allows to
experimentally evaluate and compare fuzzers via mutation analysis. As example
use cases, we assess several popular fuzzers for the Linux kernel and QEMU
executable. Mutator opens the way towards using mutation analysis as the
standard method for comparing and evaluating fuzzers.

which allows developers to easily implement custom fuzzing strategies. QFuzz
comes with three strategies: Opaque, Aggressive, and OAgg, which we evaluate
using Mutator. Besides assessing fuzzer performance, we show that the
opaqueness of the Aggressive strategy leads to improved performance on hard
crashes, while considerably reducing the search space.

strategy. We evaluate two approaches: no fuzzing of instructions that do not
write to the state (Instr) and a more fine-grained analysis that considers
functions with side effects (Funct). Our results show that Funct outperforms
Instr by more than an order of magnitude in terms of mutation detection.
Finally, we propose OAgg, a low-overhead extension of the Opaque strategy that
activates Aggressive-specific optimizations in certain situations. OAgg
outperforms Opaque by up to 25x with virtually no overhead.

standard method for comparing and evaluating fuzzers. Further, QFuzz provides
a high-level, type-safe API for executables that comes with several example
strategies, and we show that activating instructions in fuzzer strategies
leads to considerable performance gains when discovering mutations.

a popular method for estimating the true
performance of machine learning models, allowing model selection and parameter
tuning. However, the very process of CV requires random partitioning of the
data and so our performance estimates are in fact stochastic, with variability
that can be substantial for natural language processing tasks. We demonstrate
that these unstable estimates cannot be relied upon for effective parameter
tuning. The resulting tuned parameters are highly sensitive to how our data is
partitioned, meaning that we often select sub-optimal parameter choices and
have serious reproducibility issues.
  Instead, we propose to use the less variable J-K-fold CV, in which J
independent K-fold cross validations are used to assess performance. Our main
contributions are extending J-K-fold CV from performance estimation to
parameter tuning and investigating how to choose J and K. We argue that
variability is more important than bias for effective tuning and so advocate
lower choices of K than are typically seen in the NLP literature, instead use
the saved computation to increase J. To demonstrate the generality of our
recommendations we investigate a wide range of case-studies: sentiment
classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging and
document classification.
  By analysing the trade-offs between computation, bias and variability, we
provide practical recommendations for choosing J and K. Across all of the case
studied we find that tuning with J=10 and K=5 out-performs both the default
practice of K=5 and the more robust J-K-fold CV proposed in the general
literature, whilst requiring significantly less computation.
  Finally, we investigate the impact of J and K on model diversity (i.e. the
ability of different models to make different mistakes) and find that lower
choices of K lead to more diverse models.

professional knowledge work is
an understudied area. Here we investigate how public sector officials
self-assess their dependency on the Google Web search engine, whether they are
aware of the potential impact of algorithmic biases on their ability to
retrieve all relevant information, and how much relevant information may
actually be missed due to Web search personalisation. We find that the majority
of participants in our experimental study are neither aware that there is a
potential problem nor do they have a strategy to mitigate the risk of missing
relevant information when performing online searches. Most significantly, we
provide empirical evidence that up to 20% of relevant information may be missed
due to Web search personalisation. This work has significant implications for
Web research by public sector professionals, who should be provided with
training about the potential algorithmic biases that may affect their judgments
and decision making, as well as clear guidelines how to minimise the risk of
missing relevant information.
  A companion paper [1] provides a technical discussion of the Google algorithm
and its biases, followed by a qualitative investigation of how these biases
are perceived by some experts and how some experts work around them. This
response paper focuses on the impact of the algorithm's biases from the
perspective of public sector professionals who rely on Web search for their
work. It discusses how these professionals can be supported to minimize the
risk of missing relevant information when performing online searches.
  In particular, we propose training for professionals on (1) how to recognise
potential algorithmic biases, (2) how to minimise the risk of missing relevant
information, and (3) how to conduct searches to increase the likelihood of
retrieving all relevant information. We further suggest a set of guidelines,
which include using search engines other than Google, combining search results
from different search engines, and verifying information by checking it across
different sources.
  Finally, we propose the development of a search engine tailored to the needs
of public sector professionals who rely on Web search for their work. Such a
search engine could be designed to provide relevant information, independently
of any personalisation, and in a transparent way so that professionals can
effectively work around any algorithmic biases.
  We believe that these suggestions have the potential to promote more
effective online searches, and thereby support professionals working in the
public sector better in their tasks and ultimately the public at large.

  Methods: k-space data are continuously acquired using a rewound Cartesian
acquisition with spiral profile ordering (rCASPR) to provide matching contrast
to the conventional linear phase encode ordering and to sort data into multiple
respiratory phases. Low-resolution respiratory-correlated 4D images were
reconstructed with compressed sensing and used to estimate non-rigid
deformation vector fields, which were subsequently used for a motion
compensated image reconstruction. rCASPR sampling was compared to linear and
CASPR sampling in terms of point-spread-function (PSF) and image contrast with
in silico, phantom and in vivo experiments. Reconstruction parameters for
low-resolution 4D-MRI (spatial resolution and temporal regularization) were
determined using a grid search. The proposed motion compensated rCASPR was
evaluated in eight healthy volunteers and compared to free-breathing scans with
linear sampling. Image quality was compared based on visual inspection and
quantitatively by means of the gradient entropy.
  Results: rCASPR provided a superior PSF (similar in ky and narrower in kz)
and showed no considerable differences in images contrast compared to linear
sampling. The optimal 4D-MRI reconstruction parameters were a temporal
regularization of 0.05 for both linear and rCASPR samples, and a spatial
resolution of 2 x 2 x 2 mm^3 (x-y-z). Visual inspection and quantitative
measurements showed that the proposed rCASPR sampling did not impair image
quality compared to the conventional linear sampling.
  Conclusion: The proposed free-breathing 4D-MRI protocol using rCASPR is a
potential tool for resolving diaphragm and kidney boundaries better compared to
conventional linear sampling.

the Monte Carlo approximation with $20000$ samples on a common dataset.

our numerical results agree well with exact solutions already at first order in
the expansion. Moreover, the Einstein equations at first order in transverse

fields of one of these sets has only a negligible contribution to boundary
observables, such that the computation on each time slice can be simplified to
the solution of several planar shockwave equations plus four further
differential equations for each transverse plane `pixel'. At the cost of errors
of $\lesssim 10 \%$ at the hydrodynamization time and for low to mid
rapidities, useful numerical solutions can be sped up by roughly one order of
magnitude.

Hamiltonian and investigate its relation to the first order corrected Einstein
equations. Moreover, we address the relation between the transverse gradient
corrections and the coherence length of localized shocks and compare our results
to existing work.

Yang-Mills theory for a strongly coupled shock and find that transverse
gradients have a negligible effect on the pressure.
  Our results can be of great use for numerical studies of
thermodynamics, quarkonium, Higgs physics, and heavy vector boson decay in
strongly coupled theories.
  We further provide a publicly available numerical code which can be used to
compute collision physics in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory
and quantum gravity.
  We advocate for further analytical investigations of localization and
hydrodynamization in five dimensions, as there are many open questions in the
theory of shocks and hydrodynamics.
  Last but not least, we provide several ideas how transverse gradients could
be extended to higher dimensions.
  This work is also a comprehensive guide on how to perform calculations in
non-expanding AdS space.

expressive domain-specific language that describes (1) logical dependencies
between microservices, (2) patterns for the placement and configuration of
containers and their interactions, and (3) sequences of applied stresses and
failures. Additionally, Frisbee integrates a modular architecture for stressing
and failing individual nodes (faultloads) as well as the nodes' communication
links. Furthermore, Frisbee supports multiple platforms (e.g.,
Linux/ARM, Linux/x86) and languages (e.g., C++, Java, Node.js, Python).
Finally, Frisbee offers an intuitive API for developers to create tests in an
automated manner and to analyze the behavior of their applications after a
test. Through its modular design, Frisbee can be tailored to suit the testing
needs of IoT applications of various sizes and scopes.
  We evaluate Frisbee through a case study of a distributed Computer Vision
system and by measuring its performance when testing a cluster of nodes. In
conclusion, Frisbee significantly shortens the testing time for IoT applications
and provides a high degree of flexibility to developers.
  In this article, we make the following contributions: (1) we propose a
testing framework for the testing of IoT applications; (2) we introduce a
testing language that describes logical dependencies between microservices and
sequences of applied stresses and failures; (3) we present a modular architecture
for faultloads; and (4) we present a framework for the automated testing of
distributed Computer Vision systems

Existing methods typically insert actors into the scene according to a set of
hand-crafted heuristics and are limited in their ability to model the true
complexity and diversity of real traffic scenes, thus inducing a content gap
between synthesized traffic scenes versus real ones. As a result, existing
simulators lack the fidelity necessary to train and test self-driving vehicles.
To address this limitation, we present SceneGen, a neural autoregressive model
of traffic scenes that eschews the need for rules and heuristics. In
particular, given the ego-vehicle state and a high definition map of
surrounding area, SceneGen inserts actors of various classes into the scene and
synthesizes their sizes, orientations, and velocities. We demonstrate on two
large-scale datasets SceneGen's ability to faithfully model distributions of
real traffic scenes. Moreover, we show that SceneGen can be used to train
highly realistic sensor models (e.g., cameras and lidar) and rolling out
SceneGen to study scene predictability.

realistic traffic simulators, which is essential for training and validating
self-driving vehicles. To facilitate research, we provide a simulator based on
Unity that incorporates SceneGen. The simulator, called UniSim, will be made
publicly available upon acceptance of this paper.

the development and analysis of such structure-preserving discretisation
schemes, including both proofs that standard schemes have structure-preserving
properties and proposals for novel schemes that achieve both high-order
accuracy and exact preservation of certain properties of the continuum
differential equation. When coupled with implicit time-stepping methods, a
major downside to these schemes is that their structure-preserving properties
generally rely on exact solution of the (possibly nonlinear) systems of
equations defining each time-step in the discrete scheme. For small systems,
this is often possible (up to the accuracy of floating-point arithmetic), but
it becomes impractical for the large linear systems that arise when considering
typical discretisation of space-time PDEs. In this paper, we propose a
modification to the standard flexible generalised minimum residual (FGMRES)
iteration that enforces selected constraints on approximate numerical
solutions. We demonstrate its application to both systems of conservation laws
and dissipative systems.

by stellar winds and supernovae from young coeval massive star clusters within
low metallicity ($Z = 0.02$Z$_{\odot}$), clumpy molecular clouds. We explore
the initial stages of the superbubble evolution, including the occurrence of
pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae. Our aim is to study the
occurrence of dust grain growth within orbiting dusty clumps, and in the
superbubble's swept-up supershell. We also aim to address the survival of dust
grains produced by sequential supernovae. The model accounts for the star
cluster gravitational potential and self-gravity of the parent cloud. It also
considers radiative cooling (including that induced by dust) and a
state-of-the-art population synthesis model for the coeval cluster. As shown
before, a superbubble embedded into a clumpy medium becomes highly distorted,
expanding mostly due to the hot gas streaming through low density channels. Our
results indicate that in the case of massive ($\sim10^7$M$_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds, hosting a super star cluster ($\sim5.6\times10^5$M$_{\odot}$), grain
growth increments the dust mass at a rate $\sim4.8\times10^{-5}$M$_{\odot}$
over a period of $\sim15$Myr. More importantly, we find that once produced, up
to $\sim70\%$ of the SN-produced dust can become persistently trapped into the
superbubble's supershell for $\sim100$Myr, and perhaps even longer. This
predicts the possibility of a single, or perhaps a few, massive star clusters
within low-metallicity host galaxies to produce and retain a large dust
production legacy for many Gyr.
  Finally, we note that although the overall dust production is not extremely
high, the models do not account for the sub-solar dust scale lengths, delays in
the dust evolution, and the effects of additional star formation episodes
usually found in real observations. Moreover, the results are strongly dependent
on the parent cloud's initial mass, which might be over-estimated for some
galaxies. Thus, the approach reported here should be applied to a variety of
different molecular cloud models, and considering the variety of massive star
clusters, to draw more comprehensive conclusions.

3D detection (Far3Det) of objects beyond a
certain distance from an observer, e.g., $>$50m. Far3Det is particularly
important for autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating at highway speeds, which
require detections of far-field obstacles to ensure sufficient braking
distances. However, contemporary AV benchmarks such as nuScenes underemphasize
this problem because they evaluate performance only up to a certain distance
(50m). One reason is that obtaining far-field 3D annotations is difficult,
particularly for lidar sensors that produce very few point returns for far-away
objects. Indeed, we find that almost 50% of far-field objects (beyond 50m)
contain zero lidar points. Secondly, current metrics for 3D detection employ a
"one-size-fits-all" philosophy, using the same tolerance thresholds for near
and far objects, inconsistent with tolerances for both human vision and stereo
disparities. Both factors lead to an incomplete analysis of the Far3Det task.
For example, while conventional wisdom tells us that high-resolution RGB
sensors should be vital for 3D detection of far-away objects, lidar-based
methods still rank higher compared to RGB counterparts on the current benchmark
leaderboards. As a first step towards a Far3Det benchmark, we develop a method
to find well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset that contains scenes
primarily with objects beyond the 50m mark. We also introduce a model selection
framework that allows us to study the effect of sensor inputs on Far3Det. On
top of this sensor analysis, we demonstrate that by tuning the 3D tolerance
thresholds based on lidar depth, we can significantly improve detection
accuracy of far-away objects beyond 50m by about 30%. Working together, both
sensor selection and 3D tolerance tuning yield about 45% improvement on the
Far3Det problem.
