positions is a primary tool in understanding chemical reactions from first
principles. However, obtaining this information is complicated by the fact that
sampling a large number of ground states over a high-dimensional PES can
require a vast number of state preparations. In this work, we propose using a
generative quantum machine learning model to prepare quantum states at
arbitrary points on the PES. The model is trained using quantum data consisting
of ground-state wavefunctions associated with different classical nuclear
coordinates. Our approach uses a classical neural network to convert the
nuclear coordinates of a molecule into quantum parameters of a variational
quantum circuit. The model is trained using a fidelity loss function to
optimize the neural network parameters. We show that gradient evaluation is
efficient and numerically demonstrate our method's ability to prepare
wavefunctions on the PES of hydrogen chains, water, and beryllium hydride. In
all cases, we find that a small number of training points are needed to achieve
very high overlap with the groundstates in practice. From a theoretical
perspective, we further prove limitations on these protocols by showing that if
we were able to learn across an avoided crossing using a small number of
samples, then we would be able to violate Grover's lower bound. Additionally,
we prove lower bounds on the amount of quantum data needed to learn a specific
quantum circuit in our model, as well as a lower bound on the number of parameters
needed to describe the PES of hydrogen chains. Finally, we propose an
extension of our method to predict excited states and investigate its
applicability to predicting metabolic reaction rates in glucose and
fructose.

our method to larger systems by studying the circuit depth required to achieve
a certain overlap, and we find that in practice our method can be used to
predict up to several thousand nuclear coordinates. We also study the
scalability of our gradient evaluation protocol by looking at the time it takes
to compute gradients in various models and find that in practice our method can
be used to predict several hundred nuclear coordinates per hour on common
classical computers. Lastly, we propose a more efficient learning protocol that
reduces the number of required samples by several orders of magnitude in
certain cases.

review the developments in computer-assisted surgery, the applications of
non-rigid registration, and the algorithms and challenges involved in this
subject. A survey of traditional and deep-learning-based techniques is
presented. Several performance metrics are explained, and the importance of
testing registration algorithms on realistic operative data is emphasized. We
move to discuss the sources of error in soft-tissue navigation and the methods
proposed to address these challenges. Finally, we highlight the future
directions in this field and the steps towards developing perfect soft-tissue
navigation algorithms.
  Which specific algorithms or architectures are best-suited for
computer-assisted surgery? How can we improve the robustness of registration
across different datasets? How can we integrate registration into the
operative loop? How can we make the software customizable and generalizable to
different datasets and operative procedures?
  This review aims to provide an in-depth discussion of the applications,
algorithms, challenges, and future directions in soft-tissue navigation. It
can be a useful resource for both the seasoned computer-assisted surgery
professional and the inquiring researcher.
  The paper is organized into an introductory Section \ref{introduction}, an
overview of computer-assisted surgery in Section \ref{cas-review}, a discussion
of the applications, algorithms, and challenges in Sections \ref{
application-methods-challenges}, a review of deep-learning-based methods in
Section \ref{dl-methods}, a discussion of the performance metrics in
Section \ref{performance-metrics}, a review of the proposed solutions to address
the challenges in soft-tissue navigation in Section \ref{ solutions-to-challenges}
, and finally a summary of the future directions in this field in
Section \ref{future-work}.
  In order to develop perfect soft-tissue navigation algorithms, several
assumptions need to be met. First, all the relevant information needs to be
included in the images. Second, all the images needed for the operative
procedure need to be acquired before the surgery. Third, all the images are of
high-quality. Fourth, there are not any significant motion and registration is
not needed. Fifth, there are no any patient-specific variations from the
average anatomical models used for the planning and operative procedures. Sixht,
there are not any unexpected events during the operative procedures. Since
none of these assumptions are realistic, there is a need for advanced methods
that can handle various sources of error

of a dynamic 3D scene. Motion vectors have shown to be beneficial for
downstream tasks such as action classification and collision avoidance.
However, data collected via LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras are computation
and labor intensive to precisely annotate for scene flow. We address this
annotation bottleneck on two ends. We propose a 3D scene flow benchmark and a
novel self-supervised setup for training flow models. The benchmark consists of
datasets designed to study individual aspects of flow estimation in progressive
order of complexity, from a single object in motion to real-world scenes.
Furthermore, we introduce Adversarial Metric Learning for self-supervised flow
estimation. The flow model is fed with sequences of point clouds to perform
flow estimation. A second model learns a latent metric to distinguish between
the points translated by the flow estimations and the target point cloud. This
latent metric is learned via a Multi-Scale Triplet loss, which uses
intermediary feature vectors for the loss calculation. We use our proposed
benchmark to draw insights about the performance of the baselines and of
different models when trained using our setup. We find that our setup is able
to keep motion coherence and preserve local geometries, which many
self-supervised baselines fail to grasp. Dealing with occlusions, on the other
hand, is still an open challenge.

One of the major obstacles that have historically delayed large scale adoption
of ANNs is the huge computational and power costs associated with training and
testing (deploying) them. In the mean-time, Neuromorphic Computing platforms
have recently achieved remarkable performance running more bio-realistic
Spiking Neural Networks at high throughput and very low power consumption
making them a natural alternative to ANNs. Here, we propose using the Random
Neural Network (RNN), a spiking neural network with both theoretical and
practical appealing properties, as a general purpose classifier that can match
the classification power of ANNs on a number of tasks while enjoying all the
features of a spiking neural network. This is demonstrated on a number of
real-world classification datasets.
  We propose a novel algorithm to train the RNN, making it applicable to a
number of domains that were previously difficult to optimize using previous RNN
training techniques. The resulting model is tested on a number of real-world
classification datasets, showing competitive performance to state-of-the-art
ANN techniques, while being computationally and power efficient as a spiking
neural network.
  Finally, we show that the learned RNNs can be simplified into simpler
circuits, using only a few types of neurons, making them even more
efficient. This is confirmed by re-training some of the datasets directly
without hyper-parameter tuning (than the general RNN training) to achieve
higher accuracy performance, while still maintaining very low computational
and power costs.

a novel technique for automatically
learning system call filtering policies for containerized microservices
applications. At run-time, Timeloops automatically learns which system calls a
program should be allowed to invoke while rejecting attempts to call spurious
system calls. Further, Timeloops addresses many of the shortcomings of
state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques, such as the ability to
generate tight filters for programs written in interpreted languages such as
PHP, Python, and JavaScript. Timeloops has a simple and robust implementation
because it is mainly built out of commodity, and proven, technologies such as
seccomp-BPF, systemd, and Podman containers, with fewer than 500 lines of code.
We demonstrate the utility of Timeloops by learning system calls for individual
services and two microservices benchmark applications, which utilize popular
technologies like Python Flask, Nginx (with PHP and Lua modules), Apache
Thrift, Memcached, Redis, and MongoDB. Further, the amortized performance of
Timeloops is similar to that of an unhardened system while producing a smaller
system call filter than state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques.
Finally, the small footprint of the resulting filters, combined with modern
operating system technologies, such as seccomp-BPF allow for strong
protections against advanced and targeted attacks, as demonstrated by our
vulnerability experiment.

quenched disorder. This theory shows that such fluids can overcome the
disruption caused by the quenched disorder and move coherently, in the sense of
having a non-zero mean velocity in the hydrodynamic limit. However, the scaling
behavior of this class of active systems cannot be described by linearized
hydrodynamics in spatial dimensions between 2 and 5. Nonetheless, we obtain the
exact dimension-dependent scaling exponents in these dimensions.
Moreover, we find that the dynamics of fluctuations in these active systems is
described by a complex Hopf-like covariance structure, different from the
corresponding structure in usual compressible active fluids.
Finally, our results demonstrate that even though the linearized theory fails to
describe the scaling behavior of active fluids with quenched disorder, it is
still useful to understand the motion of large clusters of active particles with
quenched disorder.
This work is a detailed extension of the ideas presented in
Ref.~\cite{Tailhades2020} and incorporates several key improvements including a
full treatment of the noise in the hydrodynamic theory and the derivation of
scaling dimensions in 4 and 5 spatial dimensions.
We believe that our results provide a complete and resolved picture of
incompressible active fluids with quenched disorder and disorder-induced activity.
That is, both the scaling dimensions as well as the covariance structure of the
fluctuations are fully understood for this class of systems.
We show that the scaling behavior of active fluids with quenched disorder is
greatest in 3 spatial dimensions, where the decay of density fluctuations in
out-of-equilibrium systems with quenched disorder is the slowest possible, and
least in 2 spatial dimensions, where the scaling behavior is still interesting,
but identical to that of compressible active fluids.
Active fluids with spatial disorder move the fastest in 4 spatial dimensions and
the slowest in 2 spatial dimensions.
In 5 spatial dimensions, the motion of a active fluid with quenched disorder is
purely diffusive, just like passively advected noise.
This is similar to the scenario observed in compressible active fluids with
quenched disorder.

TESS have demonstrated that
planets are ubiquitous. However, the success of these missions heavily depends
on ground-based radial velocity (RV) surveys, which combined with transit
photometry can yield bulk densities and orbital properties. While most Kepler
host stars are too faint for detailed follow-up observations, TESS is detecting
planets orbiting nearby bright stars that are more amenable to RV
characterization. Here we introduce the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV program
using ~100 nights on Keck/HIRES to study exoplanets identified by TESS. The
primary survey aims are investigating the link between stellar properties and
the compositions of small planets; studying how the diversity of system
architectures depends on dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity;
identifying prime candidates for atmospheric studies with JWST; and
understanding the role of stellar evolution in shaping planetary systems. We
present a fully-automated target selection algorithm, which yielded 103 planets
in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. Most TKS hosts are inactive,
solar-like, main-sequence stars (4500 K < Teff < 6000 K) at a wide range of
metallicities. The selected TKS sample contains 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re),
11 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 6 sub-day period planets and 3
planets in the habitable zone. The TKS sample is generally free of strong
stellar activity indicators, but activity levels are not uniformly low. We
find a significant correlation between the Nearest Neighbor Distance (NND) of
the sample hosts in the Teff-[Fe/H] plane and the fraction of systems with
multi-transiting candidates. We conclude that this correlation is likely due
to the detection bias against active, wide-separation multi-planetary systems
that are easily distinguished from background eclipse mimics. Finally, we find
that systems with NND > 2 are 3 times more likely to have a planet with a
period between 2 and 10 days. The TKS sample appears to be under-sampled for
investigating planet composition as a function of stellar metallicity, and
future RV surveys should consider the interaction between activity and metal
content when selecting targets.

Let $L(s,\chi)$ be the Dirichlet $L$-function corresponding to a Dirichlet
character $\chi$ of some prime $k \geq 2$. The zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ are
conjugate symmetric complex numbers in the critical strip $0<\mathrm{Re}(s)<1$.
It is conjectured that all nontrivial zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ lie within the critical
strip. In particular, the conjecture implies that there are no zeros on the
line $\mathrm{Re}(s)=1$. A \emph{Landau-Siegel zero} (or simply \emph{LSZ} for
short) for $L(s,\chi)$ is a zero that lies on the line $\mathrm{Re}(s)=1$.
Dirichlet characters $\chi$ for which there are Landau-Siegel zeros are of
particular interest, and their nonexistence has been established unconditionally
by Dirichlet's theorem when $|\chi|$ $=k$ is prime and $k \geq 3$. Landau
\cite{Landau} showed that there are no Landau-Siegel zeros for Dirichlet $L$-functions

when reasoning about pairs of programs, our logic allows us to quantitatively

  Our logic includes a novel quantitative semantics for "expectations" -- which
are pre- and postconditions that refer to the relational operator -- that
captures their failure probability. The semantics is fragile in Hoare logic
because changing even a single quantitative label can make many steps no longer
apply. Thus our core contribution is showing that despite this fragility, the
quantitative semantics remains stable throughout a proof.
  To achieve this, we show a "repair rule" that applies to many steps in our
proof system to refocus them to the part of the expectation that is actually
relevant to the step. This rule uses the structure of quantum Hoare logic to
turn quantitative information into qualitative information about relations,
allowing us to use many steps from (Unruh, POPL 2019) directly in our proofs.
  We also introduce a new axiomatization of quantum Hoare logic which is more
practical for our proof system; in particular, it avoids a problematic axiom
that is often needed to derive derivations that lead to superoperators that
"overlook" parts of the pre-/postcondition. Finally, we show soundness and
completeness of our logic w.r.t. a natural class of superoperators that capture
our notion of "expectation".
  Putting it all together, our proof system allows us to write concise proofs
about programs that interact with other programs; these proofs capture precise
information about how much the interactions succeed, and the methodology of
applying our proof system is illustrated through a series of examples.
Furthermore, the steps in our proof system correspond to steps in classical
relational Hoare logic, making it easy to translate proofs from classical Hoare
logic into our system.
  In conclusion, our logic and proof system provide a practical way to reason
about programs that relate to other programs, combining the benefits of
quantum Hoare logic and classical relational Hoare logic.

ially private stochastic gradient
descent (DPSGD) is a fundamental challenge. Unlike the typical SGD, private
datasets cannot be used many times for hyperparameter search in DPSGD; e.g.,
via a grid search. Therefore, there is an essential need for algorithms that,
within a given search space, can find near-optimal hyperparameters for the best
achievable privacy-utility tradeoffs efficiently. We formulate this problem
into a general optimization framework for establishing a desirable
privacy-utility tradeoff, and systematically study three cost-effective
algorithms: evolutionary, Bayesian optimization, and Proximal Adaptive
Gradient. Our experiments show that these algorithms outperform the baseline
grid search substantially, in terms of both convergence time and utility
tradeoffs. As this is the first study of hyperparameter tuning in private
deep learning, our framework and methods are generally applicable to any DPSGD
implementation.
  We also study how different privacy mechanisms - the DPSGD and the
Differential Privacy with Wavelet Stretching (DPWS) - over the search space
affect the tradeoffs. We train a pre-trained ConvNet on the private MNIST
dataset using DPSGD and also on the private, compressed MNIST dataset using
DPWS. Our analysis shows that the DPWS is more robust to hyperparameter
variations than the DPSGD, and thus, the need for careful hyperparameter
tuning is even more pronounced in DPSGD.
  Finally, we study how the proposed tuning algorithms affect the privacy
tradeoffs. We examine the leak of information (loosely speaking, the
privacy) from the parameter values (hyperparameters) to the raw data points in
a private dataset. We show that certain hyperparameters more significantly
affect the privacy than the others; and the tuning algorithms generally search
for the hyperparameters that maximize the privacy (thus, they often converge
to the same value of the hyperparameter) as soon as they find a local
minimum. Moreover, we also examine the leak of information from the data to
the parameter values (tighter bounds on privacy) and show that the proposed
tuning algorithms do not increase the probability of rare privacy breaches
significantly (thus, they are privacy-preserving).
  The proposed framework and the tuning algorithms are generally applicable to
all private deep learning problems (hyperparameters learning, training deep
neural networks, etc.). Moreover, the analysis of the privacy tradeoffs is

Virus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic swept the
world.In China, COVID-19 has caused severe consequences. Moreover, online
rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic increased people's panic about public
health and social stability. At present, understanding and curbing the spread
of online rumors is an urgent task. Therefore, we analyzed the rumor spreading
mechanism and propose a method to quantify a rumors' influence by the speed of
new insiders. The search frequency of the rumor is used as an observation
variable of new insiders. The peak coefficient and the attenuation coefficient
are calculated for the search frequency, which conforms to the exponential
distribution. We designed several rumor features and used the above two
coefficients as predictable labels. A 5-fold cross-validation experiment using
the mean square error (MSE) as the loss function showed that the decision tree
was suitable for predicting the peak coefficient, and the linear regression
model was ideal for predicting the attenuation coefficient. Our feature
analysis showed that precursor features were the most important for the
outbreak coefficient, while location information and rumor entity information
were the most important for the attenuation coefficient. Meanwhile, features
that were conducive to the outbreak were usually harmful to the continued
spread of rumors. At the same time, anxiety was a crucial rumor causing factor.
Finally, we discuss how to use deep learning technology to reduce the forecast
loss by combining the model with a neural network. This study proposes two
predictive indicators for online rumors and gives them specific interpretations
based on the experiment, which is beneficial to understand the mechanism of
rumor spreading and curb the spread of rumors.

interest to subject this data to statistical analysis to gain more insights and
provide improved medical diagnoses. Such analyses require complex computations
on large volumes of data, demanding efficient data processing systems. This
paper shows that currently available data processing solutions either fail to
meet the performance requirements or lack simple and flexible programming
interfaces. To address this problem, we propose \emph{LifeStream}, a
high-performance stream processing engine for physiological data. LifeStream
hits the sweet spot between ease of programming by providing a rich temporal
query language support and performance by employing optimizations that exploit
the periodic nature of physiological data. We demonstrate that LifeStream

streaming engines and $3.2\times$ than hand-optimized numerical libraries on

  Hospital patients generate vast amounts of continuous physiological data
through non-invasive monitoring devices while receiving treatment. Analyzing
and processing this data over time can lead to better understanding of diseases
and improvements in healthcare delivery. However, frequent hardware faults
make it challenging to provide reliable services for physiological data analysis
over time. To address this issue, we propose \emph{FaultStream}, a fault-tolerant
stream processing engine for physiological data. FaultStream effectively
eliminates temporary failures from streaming applications by providing automatic
fault detection, temporary failure recovery, and high availability through
replication without the need for custom failure handling code. It achieves this
by exploiting the periodic nature of physiological data and the semantics of
applications that process it. We demonstrate that FaultStream achieves up to
$4.8\times$ lower recovery latency, $2.2\times$ higher system availability,
and significant performance benefits compared to existing fault-tolerant stream
processing engines.

which involves extending the definition of the correlation function of the

addition to the PCM, we present three other popular correlation functions

different correlation functions were tested in the present work to solve the
passive scalar transport equation with the RANS equations for various
non-reactive flow configurations. It was found that the PCM was the most
accurate of the tested correlation functions for all of the tested cases. This
idea of extending the definition of the correlation function of the scalar to
the fluid particles is a novel concept which has not been previously reported

International Beamline for Extreme Fields (HIBEF) at the European X-ray Free
Electron Laser (XFEL), we calculate the birefringent scattering of x-rays at
the combined field of two optical (or near-optical) lasers and compare various
scenarios. In order to facilitate an experimental detection of quantum vacuum
diffraction and birefringence, special emphasis is placed on scenarios where
the initial and final x-ray photons differ not just in polarization, but also
in propagation direction (corresponding to scattering angles in the mrad
regime) and possibly energy.
  In all scenarios considered here the effect of birefringence is found to be
substantial, with elastic and quasi-elastic scattering processes contributing
most to the effect. Non-elastic processes, though negligible in the cross
section, accumulate in the electromagnetic fields and may thus become
significant in the birefringent phase shift. Scenarios where the x-ray beam
makes large angles with the optical beams (above about 5 deg) reduce the
effect, while scenarios where also the energy of the x-ray photons is allowed
to vary shows the best prospects for an experimental detection of
birefringence. This includes scenarios where deep inside the interaction region
the x-ray beam is focused onto a tiny spot by means of a diffractive lens
imprinted with a microstructure sensitive to the optical fields.
  In addition to a discussion of the birefringent phase shift, we present a
full quantitative analysis of the scattering processes involved and estimate
the experimental signatures that can be expected. While the cross sections of
the processes involved are in general very small, the high fluxes of x-rays
expected at present and future XFEL facilities may still yield a number of
scattered photons sufficient to signal birefringence or quantum vacuum diffraction
with good certainty. In order to facilitate such an experimental detection, we
present several scenarios for the design of the HIBEF beamline and discuss in
which ways the selection of detection channels and the use of diffractive
lenses may contribute to an optimal observation of birefringence and quantum
vacuum diffraction.
  Finally, we compare our results to recent theoretical work on
x-ray birefringence and quantum vacuum diffraction induced by optical fields,
and discuss limitations and areas for future improvement.

encryption scheme with the following attractive feature: given a ciphertext, an
adversary cannot create two ciphertexts both of which decrypt to the same
message as the original ciphertext. We revisit this notion and show the
following:
  - Reusability: The constructions proposed by Broadbent and Lord have the
disadvantage that they either guarantee one-time security (that is, the
encryption key can only be used once to encrypt the message) in the plain model
or they guaranteed security in the random oracle model. We construct unclonable
encryption schemes with semantic security. We present two constructions (for
public-key and private-key settings) from minimal cryptographic assumptions.
  - Lower Bound and Generalized Construction: We revisit the
information-theoretic one-time secure construction of Broadbent and Lord. The
success probability of the adversary in their construction was guaranteed to be
$0.85^n$, where $n$ is the length of the message. It was interesting to
understand whether the ideal success probability of (negligibly close to)
$0.5^n$ was unattainable. We generalize their construction to be based on a
broader class of monogamy of entanglement games. We demonstrate a simple
cloning attack that succeeds with probability $0.71^n$ against a class of
schemes that Broadbent and Lord built to guarantee one-time secure unclonable
encryption from this class of constructions. We then demonstrate a complexity
theoretic argument showing that the ideal success probability of $0.5^n$ is
most likely unattainable in this complexity world.

messages of a single block of plain text. For enclosing security guarantees for
multiple blocks of plain text, one could think of using a cryptographic
encryption scheme to encrypt the plain text. However, this would lose the
feature of unclonable encryption. We construct a scheme that guarantees
unclonability and security even if the message consists of multiple blocks of
plain text.

information-theoretic authentication in additive white Gaussian noise channels,

encoder, decoder, and adversary, where the adversary has access to the message,
a non-causal noisy observation of the encoder's transmission, and unlimited
transmission power, while the decoder observes a noisy version of the sum of

modification costs an asymptotically negligible amount of the coding rate,
while still enabling authentication as long as the adversary's observation is
not noiseless. Also notable is that this modification is not (asymptotically) a
function of the statistical characterization of the adversary's channel and
furthermore no secret key is required, hence paving the way for a robust

an expansive wind outflow, often
constrained or channeled by magnetic fields that form a surrounding
magnetosphere. The very strong winds of massive stars are understood to be
driven by line-scattering of the star's radiative momentum, while in the Sun
and even lower-mass stars a much weaker mass loss arises from the thermal
expansion of a mechanically heated corona. In exoplanets around such low-mass
stars, the radiative heating and wind interaction can lead to thermal expansion
or mechanical ablation of their atmospheres. Stellar magnetospheres result from
the internal trapping of the wind outflow, while planetary magnetospheres are
typically shaped by the external impact from the star's wind. But in both cases
the stressing can drive magnetic reconnection that results in observable
signatures such as X-ray flares and radio outbursts. This review will aim to
give an overview of the underlying physics of these processes with emphasis on
their similarities and distinctions for stars vs. planets.
  We find that there is a considerable lack of common terminology in the
literature that differentiates stellar and planetary cases. This lack of
distinction likely leads to confusion in the audience not familiar with either
stellar or planetary physics. To address this, we provide a detailed
comparison of the relevant parameters such as the relative wind speed, the
importance of the self-gravity of the outflow, and the mechanical vs.
therapeutic (radiative) heating of the target atmosphere.
  It is clear that the distinction between these different physical
configurations is not a binary stellar vs. planetary one, but rather a
continuum from stellar to planetary and beyond (to asteroids and comets). It
is imperative that the community adopts a universal terminology to facilitate
communication and comparison between the different cases.
  Finally, the understanding and modeling of these processes can be improved
and made more relevant to exoplanets by more extensive observational work on
our own Sun and heliosphere. Conversely, the use of analogies between stars
and exoplanets can be improved by examining the parameters and processes that
differ between them.

layer near to a heavy metal. It has been seen in several stackings, and is
usually explained by the hybridization between the layer of interest and the
heavy metal. However, the Crossover between the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect
and the Strain (or Biaxial-Strain) in II-VI and III-V semiconductors is not
fully clear. In this work, we explain the Crossover between Strain and
Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in a GaAs/AlGaAs structure by the combination of
two effects: the Hybridization and the Elastic Strain
Spin-Other-Orbit Coupling. The Hybridization is responsible for the large
increase of the $\Gamma$-valley spin-orbit splitting in thin GaAs layers
grown on AlGaAs, while the Elastic Strain Spin-Other-Orbit Coupling is
responsible for the increase of the spin-orbit splitting in thick GaAs layers
and for the Crossover between both effects for a given valley and spin state.
This Crossover happens in agreement with experimental results.
Furthermore, we explain how the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and the Biaxial
Strain can be tuned by changing the thickness of the GaAs layer and the lattice
mismatch between the two materials.
Finally, our results open the possibility of growing layers for quantum computing
and other applications where a large and tunable Spin-Other-Orbit Coupling is
needed.
Concretely, by controlling the Biaxial Strain, the $\Gamma$-valley spin-orbit
splitting can be turned off or strongly increased depending on the GaAs thickness.
This could be useful for qubits that use the $\Gamma$ valley, and could
improve the efficiency of qubits that need a large spin-orbit coupling. The
hysteresis of the spin-orbit splitting because of the lattice mismatch could
also be useful, once controlled, to design switches for the spin other orbit

properties of all the nouns in a sentence. At the same time, it is regular:

(PET) imaging limits its
usage in the studies of radiation-sensitive populations, e.g., pregnant women,
children, and adults that require simultaneous radiation dose and efficacy
optimization in medical treatments. To develop effective dose-reduced PET
imaging protocols, it is critical to understand the effects of partial dose
acquisition on PET image quality, system performance, and quantification accuracy
for large and small subjects. In this work, we investigated the impact of
split-dose acquisition (half of the standard dose per bed position) on
transaxial, axial, and cylindrical (whole-body) image quality for adult and
pediatric subjects. To evaluate image quality, we analyzed the system performance
(in-plane resolution, axial resolution, verbial sensitivity), and quantification
accuracy (mean absolute percentage error or MAPE) for hot and cold objects,
reconstructed from scans acquired at split and full dose. Our results show that
for adult and pediatric subjects, split-dose reconstruction produces images
with similar or slightly better quality compared to full-dose reconstruction.
In particular, the split-dose protocol yields significant improvements in
image resolution (in-plane and axial) and quantification accuracy for small
objects. For large objects, image resolution and quantification accuracy are
maintained with the split-dose protocol. To further evaluate the effect of
split-dose on image quality a figure-of-merit (FOM) was defined based on
subjective rating of experienced engineers and physicists. Subjective FOM
scores indicate that images obtained with the split-dose protocol are of
equivalent or slightly better quality than those obtained with the full-dose
protocol. We also observed that split-dose reconstruction does not significantly
degrade whole-body image quality, even when only half of the standard acquisition
time is used. Our findings suggest split-dose protocols are promising for
reducing the effective dose in PET imaging across a variety of subjects.

temperature dependence of
sticking forces between micrometer grains of chondritic composition. The data
showed a decrease in surface energy by a factor ~5 with increasing temperature.
Here, we focus on the effect of surface water on grains. Under ambient
conditions in the laboratory, multiple water layers are present. At the low
pressure of protoplanetary discs and for moderate temperatures, grains likely
only hold a monolayer. As dust drifts inwards, even this monolayer eventually
evaporates completely in higher temperature regions. To account for this, we
measured the tensile strength for the same chondritic material as was prepared
and measured under normal laboratory conditions in our previous work, but now
introducing two new preparation methods: drying dust cylinders in air (dry
samples), and heating dust pressed into cylinders in vacuum (super-dry
samples). For all temperatures up to 1000 K, the data of the dry samples are
consistent with a simple increase in the sticking force by a factor of ~10 over
wet samples. Up to 900 K super-dry samples behave like dry samples. However,
the sticking forces then exponentially increase up to another factor ~100 at
about 1200 K. The increase in sticking from wet to dry extends our previous
finding of a decrease of surface energy with temperature to higher
temperatures. The increase in sticking for super-dry samples at even higher
temperatures is consistent with a phase transition to a stickier, more water
rich state at depths where water has not yet evaporated. Our results strongly
improve the understanding and modelling of dust growth and mixing in
protoplanetary discs.
  Based on our laboratory results, we discuss modifications to dust growth
models. Unlike previous laboratory experiments, our results for the sticking
forces at low temperatures (up to 1000 K) are compatible with the conditions
found in the outer disc. There, growth is expected to be controlled by
gravity, and our data demonstrate that, in the presence of a monolayer of
water, the sticking forces are high enough to quickly collapse dust aggregates
into centimeter-sized bodies or larger. These objects, called pebbles, are
included in models as already grown bodies, but our data suggest they rather
form directly in the outer disc. Furthermore, we advise models to include a
disc region around 0.5 au where growth is halted due to the evaporating
monolayer.

generation, imitation learning has been viewed as a vital direction in the
context of robot skill learning. In contrast to unconstrained imitation
learning which ignores possible internal and external constraints arising from
environments and robot kinematics/dynamics, recent works on constrained
imitation learning allow for transferring human skills to unstructured
scenarios, further enlarging the application domain of imitation learning.
While various constraints have been studied, e.g., joint limits, obstacle
avoidance and plane constraints, the problem of nonlinear hard constraints has
not been well-addressed. In this paper, we propose extended kernelized movement
primitives (EKMP) to cope with most of the key problems in imitation learning,
including nonlinear hard constraints. Specifically, EKMP is capable of learning
the probabilistic features of multiple demonstrations, adapting the learned
skills towards arbitrary desired points in terms of joint position and
velocity, avoiding obstacles at the level of robot links, as well as satisfying
arbitrary linear and nonlinear, equality and inequality hard constraints.
Besides, the connections between EKMP and state-of-the-art motion planning
approaches are discussed. Several evaluations including the planning of joint
trajectories for a 7-DoF robotic arm are provided to verify the effectiveness
of our framework.

for discovering wide separation binary asteroids in wide field surveys. We then
applied these techniques to images of main belt asteroids in the 4 to 60 km
size range captured by Pan-STARRS1. Johnston (2019) lists fewer than 10 known
binaries in this size range with separations greater than 10% of the primary's
Hill radius, so discovering more wide binary asteroids is crucial for
understanding the limits of binary stability and improving our knowledge of
asteroid masses. We analyzed each image by: i) comparing the major axis
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF to its non-sidereal rate on the
sky, and ii) comparing the one-dimensional median profile created by collapsing
the image along the asteroid's direction of motion to that of nearby field
stars. For both methods, we flagged any results that deviated significantly
from the expected measurements of single asteroids, and those targets with the
most flags were identified as binary candidates for confirmation with
high-acuity imaging.
  Both techniques yielded several binary candidates, but the results were
affected by the limitations of the analysis methods as well as the quality of
the input images. Nevertheless, we were able to confirm the composition of 3
out of 6 of our top candidates using Keck II/OSIRIS. Two of the confirmed
binaries, (1685) Toro and (2829) Xiaoqingcao, are near-Earth asteroids that
move rapidly enough to have avoided collisions with the Earth-Moon system and
planetary objects with radii greater than 100 km during the last 300 kyr. The
third confirmed binary, (1700) Apple, is a M-type asteroid that moves in a
distinctly non-gravitational path within the main belt. We will present the
final confirmation results and discuss the characteristics of binary
asteroids that our techniques are best suited to discover.

spin alignment of partons inside hadrons and investigate the origins, roles,

and SIDIS processes. The parton spin alignment functions are the extensions of
the Boer-Mulders function and can be associated with the collective alignment
of quark spin vectors. The proposed functions are different from the Desselsohn-Mulders function
and the Sivers function, which are all initiated by the interactions encoded in
the corresponding correlators. The parton spin alignment functions are
propelled by the spin alignments of partons inside hadrons and are sensitive to

investigated in the future EIC and COMPASS experiments through Drell-Yan and

wearable devices such as
smart phones and wristbands make it easy to get access to people's health
information including activities, sleep, sports, etc. Smart healthcare achieves
great success by training machine learning models on a large quantity of user
data. However, there are two critical challenges. Firstly, user data often
exists in the form of isolated islands, making it difficult to perform
aggregation without compromising privacy security. Secondly, the models trained
on the cloud fail on personalization. In this paper, we propose FedHealth, the
first federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare to tackle
these challenges. FedHealth performs data aggregation through federated
learning, and then builds personalized models by transfer learning. It is able
to achieve accurate and personalized healthcare without compromising privacy
and security. Experiments demonstrate that FedHealth produces higher accuracy
(5.3% improvement) for wearable activity recognition when compared to
traditional methods. FedHealth is general and extensible and has the potential
to be used in many healthcare applications.

to be missed by these approaches and may also be relevant for understanding the

of a nucleon is smaller, whereas the one-body potential is stronger, than in
non-relativistic models. The product of those two quantities is about the same
in both approaches. From the sum rule of the neutron effective mass, the
density dependence of the symmetry potential is constrained. With that
constraint, the neutron skin predicted by the density dependent relativistic
mean field model is about 0.2 fm thinner than that calculated in non-relastic
models.
  A simple relativistic model in which the nucleon effective mass is a function
of the nuclear matter density is proposed. In that model, the density dependence
of the neutron skin is self-consistently generated from the density dependence
of the effective neutron mass. The predicted value of the skin at normal
density is about 0.2 fm thinner than the non-relativistic calculation has.
Additional features of that model are that it has a good binding energy at
normal density and that it satisfies the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem.

although the neutron skin at subnormal temperatures is a little bit thicker
than at normal density in the models used. The prediction of the finite
temperature model for the point neutron radius at various temperatures is
consistent with the data of the Hubble-type observation assuming the normal
density of nuclear matter.

Bayesian neural network model. It is found that it is a little bit thicker
than at normal density, in agreement with the finite temperature model.

is a new and important research area in the larger
field of machine learning. With CDL, researchers aim to structure and encode
causal knowledge in the extremely flexible representation space of deep
learning models. Doing so will lead to more informed, robust, and general
predictions and inference -- which is important! However, CDL is still in its
infancy. For example, it is not clear how we ought to compare different methods
as they are so different in their output, the way they represent causal
information, and even their output distribution. This is a living paper that
surveys the current landscape of CDL, identifies classes of methods, and
proposes a novel framework for comparing CDL methods. We define a new class of
methods, called causal embedding methods, and provide a comprehensive survey of
existing methods for causal embedding learning, pre-training, and assessment.
Furthermore, we introduce a novel framework for comparing CDL methods, called
Meta-CausalSpace, which encodes a mapping between a set of tasks and a
representation space, via a transformer encoder. Meta-CausalSpace allows to
solve inference in CDL, i.e., given a set of methods and tasks, which method
predicts the causal feature representation of a new instance? We validate
Meta-CausalSpace on various datasets and learning settings, and we release our
code and datasets at \url{https://github.com/ericksonmg/causal-deep-learning}.
  From our experiments, we observe that there is a clear gap between different
CDL methods, even when they are trained on the same data. Moreover, we observe
that the prediction of single tasks is often already very good, but we are far
from generalization, even when we pre-train on numerous datasets. This is
encouraging, as simply adding more data and better architectures will likely
lead to more informed and robust predictions. Finally, we observe that the
assessing CDL methods is non-trivial, and we need more sophisticated metrics,
including those that compare the functional relationship between the input and
causal output representation.

is crucial for yield optimization and process stability. Yet, in situ
temperature measurements with spatial and temporal resolution are still
challenging. In this work, we perform temperature measurements in a cylindrical
fixed bed reactor by combining the capabilities of real-time magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) with the temperature-dependent proton resonance frequency (PRF)
shift of water. Three-dimensional (3D) temperature maps are acquired while
heating the bed from room temperature to 60~$^{\circ}$C using hot air. The
obtained results show a clear temperature gradient along the axial and radial
dimensions and agree with optical temperature probe measurements with an
average error of $\pm$ 1.5~$^{\circ}$C. We believe that the MR thermometry
methodology presented here opens new perspectives for the fundamental study of
mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds and in the future might be

by the equations of three-dimensional finite elasticity, which are discretized

or even superior to the AMG one for cardiac mechanics. However, the best
performance is achieved when the computation of the local solvers in the BDDC
algorithm is done by a direct solver that is highly efficient for symmetric
linear systems; this is a common practice in other DDMs for other problems and

work demonstrates the effectiveness of BDDC preconditioners for cardiac mechanics

the nonlinear interactions between the walkers. The scenarios here described and

involving the Albanese quotient of $\mathcal{V}$.

In this work, we present our results on the ARID dataset. Most previous works
only evaluate performance on large, well illuminated datasets like Kinetics and
HMDB51. We demonstrate that our work is able to achieve a very low error rate
while being trained on a much smaller dataset of dark videos. We also explore a
variety of training and inference strategies including domain transfer
methodologies and also propose a simple but useful frame selection strategy.
Our empirical results demonstrate that we beat previously published baseline
models by 11%.
  We also investigate the effect of adding illuminance information to the models.
While it is intuitive to assume that the models should be able to ignore
illuminess, we find that it does have an effect. Thus, we propose a very
simple methodology to add illuminance information to the data without increasing
its dimensionality. This gives us a nice boost of 6%.
  Finally, we also explore the effect of supervised learning of dark videos in
presence of overexposure and underexposure frames. We observe that the models
tend to be unbalanced in their error distribution with a majority of errors on
underexposure frames. Thus, we propose a simple but efficient strategy to
filter overexposure frames during inference. This gives us a nice boost of 4%.
Our empirical results demonstrate that our models are able to achieve a very low
error rate compared to strong baselines.

the implementation of a Content
Addressable Parallel Processor using a FPGA. While Content addressable memories
have been implemented in FPGAs, to our knowledge this is the first
implementation in FPGA of Caxton C. Foster's vision of parallel processing,
particularly the notions of parallel write as well as the combining of output
values, which are usually missing in more typical CAM implementations, such as
the ones designed for network routing. The resulting CAPP is made accessible to
a host computer over a USB/UART interface, using a straightforward serial
protocol that is demonstrated using a Python-based driver.
  The CAPP consists of 256 x 64 bits, with 64 parallel output ports, and takes
a latency of three FPGA clock cycles (approximately 10 ns) to find and write
to a target address. The write operation involves both a 64-bit data value to
be written to the target location as well as a 8-bit `glue' value that
determines how the output values to be combined (overwritten) are mapped,
ranging from `no change' to `map to the register that the written value came
from'. The combining operation is programmable via a 256 x 8 glues ROM
embedded into the FPGA. The CAPP has been tested extensively while embedded
into a FPGA development board (Cypress PSoC 6 MCU one) using the
Segger J-Link USB connector for interaction with Python. The test suite includes
over 120 distinct test cases as well as a thorough analysis of the searching
latency over a large number of random target addresses as well as over random
target addresses with a mix search keys embedded into the CAPP's glues ROM.
Finally, we include a Python driver that fully utilises the CAPP's parallel
output feature, thus demonstrating the ease of use of this CAPP via its
serial (UART) interface.
  In summary, this CAPP implementation showcases an interesting and
non-traditional FPGA design project, which could serve as a nice educative
activity for electronics and computer engineering students, particularly those
interested in VHDL/DV development as well as computer architecture. The complete
VHDL source code is freely available upon request to the authors.

detecting anomalous data
samples in streams of data. This problem poses challenges that classical and
deep anomaly detection methods are designed to tackle. One such challenge is
handling evolving data distributions. Most existing approaches assume that the
underlying data distribution does not change over time and focus on
accumulating knowledge from past data to make predictions on future data.
However, in streaming anomaly detection, past data are typically discarded
since they do not change over time. Thus, these approaches cannot leverage the
past data to make predictions on stream data. Furthermore, they can also be
considered as semi-parametric approaches that parametric and non-parametric
components work together to handle evolving data distributions. Recently, a
semi-parametric streaming anomaly detection algorithm that uses a parametric
clustering model to represent normal data and a non-parametric memory to
store past normal data samples was proposed. In this work, we study this
algorithm and its components, and show that it is at least as good as other
streaming anomaly detection algorithms. We also propose a new version of the
algorithm that uses a non-parametric clustering model to represent normal data
and a parametric memory to store past normal data samples. We evaluate this
algorithm on a dataset of system calls extracted from Linux servers, and show
that it outperforms the baseline algorithm.
  Anomaly detection refers to the task of identifying data samples in a
dataset that are anomalous with respect to the rest of the data in the
dataset. Streaming anomaly detection refers to the anomaly detection problem
when the data to be analyzed is received item by item, rather than all at once.
Many streaming anomaly detection algorithms use a distance function to measure
the similarity of data samples and consider as anomalous any data sample that
exceeds a threshold on that distance measure. In this work, we study one such
algorithm that also uses clustering as a way to adapt to evolving data
distributions. We show that this algorithm makes predictions based on its
concept of normality and that its performance is determined by its clustering
quality. We also show that this algorithm can be made more efficient by
modifying the updated formula for the distance measure. By experiments on six
datasets, we show that this modification yields an order of magnitude gain in
performance without a loss in accuracy.

formalisms, we propose demonstrability as a new central concept for describing
compelled acts. We additionally provide a language for whether a compelled
action meaningfully entails the respondent to perform in a manner that is 'as
good as' the government's desired goal. Then, we apply our definitions to
analyze the compellability of several cryptographic primitives including
decryption, multifactor authentication, commitment schemes, and hash functions.
In particular, our framework reaches a novel conclusion about compelled
decryption in the setting that the encryption scheme is deniable: the
government can compel but the respondent is free to use this information to
extract the plaintext in a way that leaves no evidence of the assistance of
the password.

illustrate the central importance of the notion of 'failure' in cryptographic
primitives. In particular, we show that this notion determines whether a

beyond. For Max-CSPs, and even more generally, maximisation finite-valued CSPs
(where constraints are arbitrary non-negative functions), Romero, Wrochna, and

simple PTAS for all fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes, which is the most
general "sparsity" condition for which a PTAS is known. We extend these results
to general-valued CSPs, which include "crisp" (or "strict") constraints that
have to be satisfied by every feasible assignment. The only condition on the
crisp constraints is that their domain contains an element which is at least as
feasible as all the others (but possibly less optimal).
  For minimisation general-valued CSPs with crisp constraints, we present a
PTAS for all Baker graph classes -- a definition by Dvo\v{r}\'ak [SODA'20]
which encompasses all classes where Baker's technique is known to work, except
possibly for fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. This extends to "yes-in-no"
instances of general-valued CSPs, i.e., instances where it is easy to find at
least one feasible assignment that satisfies all the crisp constraints.
  Our key insight is to translate crisp constraints into "pseudo-variables",
whose value determines a subset of the variables that satisfy all the crisp
constraints. This allows us to reduce the original constraint satisfaction
problem to a set of "shadow" constraints, and to apply the usual PTAS
techniques. Another important insight is to handle the interaction between the
shadow constraints and the optimal value of the instance. This interaction
affects the analysis of a PTAS, as it does indeed in the case of fractionally
treewidth-fragile classes. In our case, the sparsity condition ensuring the
existence of a PTAS is even stronger, but the analysis still works exactly as
in the case of Max-CSPs.

detection of a nonmonotonic radial
rotation profile in a low-mass lower-luminosity giant star. For most low- and
intermediate-mass stars, the rotation on the main sequence seems to be close to
rigid. As these stars evolve into giants, the core contracts and the envelope
expands, which should suggest a radial rotation profile with a fast core and a
slower envelope and surface. KIC 9267654, however, seems to show a surface
rotation rate that is faster than its bulk envelope rotation rate, in conflict
with this simple angular momentum conservation argument. We improve the
spectroscopic surface constraint, show that the pulsation frequencies are
consistent with the previously published core and envelope rotation rates, and
demonstrate that the star does not show strong chemical peculiarities. We
discuss the evidence against any tidally interacting stellar companion.
Finally, we discuss the possible origin of this unusual rotation profile,
including the potential ingestion of a giant planet or unusual angular momentum
transport by tidal inertial waves triggered by a close substellar companion,
and encourage further observational and theoretical efforts.
  KIC 9267654 is a Kepler target that we classify as a giant of approximately
1.56 $M_\odot$ and 3.5 $R_\odot$, based on its surface activity,
multimodal spectral analysis, and evolutionary modeling. Its surface rotation
rate of 72.1 $\pm$ 1.0 d$^{-1}$ makes it one of the fastest known giant branch
rotators. A non-tidal stellar rotation radial profile is usually expected for
short-period multiple star systems only, for which the outermost layer is
truly tidally locked. To our knowledge, KIC 9267654 has not been previously
reported as a multiple star system, and its broad Asiago Automated Telescope
ASTRA survey spectra do not show any clear companion signature within $\sim$
0.13 lt-day. The Feh-EnCen spectral analysis that we performed returns a metal
licity [Fe/H] = $-$0.76 $\pm$ 0.07, which is not unusual for this mass. A
long-baseline interferometric characterization of this object would greatly
help to assess the extent of its nonmonotonic rotation profile.

guarantee of sparsity. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm, named

posteriori adapted to the data. The selection is performed by a pure categorical
approach, unlike the Flexible Lasso, which considers a continuous scale to
measure the sparsity. The estimation of the relevant factors is performed by a
global approach, unlike the Monotone Group Lasso, which considers the units as
an ordered set. Furthermore, our algorithm considers a simple penalization
scheme, unlike the Flexible Lasso, which requires a complex norm optimization.

and their levels for each selected factor. We show its applicability in the
analysis of a real data set and compare it with other selection models, namely
the Logistic Regression, the Firth algorithm for the Bayesian information
critera and the Group Lasso.

smaller size KG, WikiMovies, we saw 3x improvement of exact match score on

no alignment between the knowledge graph and text corpus is required in
curating training data. This makes our method particularly useful when working
with industry-scale knowledge graphs.

triples from multiple knowledge graphs. The idea is to exploit the differences
in the coverage and quality of different KGs. Our experiments show that the
models gain higher performance on tasks that cover multiple graphs than
individual models. Exploring other ways of combining single-KG models and
further analyzing the phenomenon are interesting directions for future work.

ophysical computational model of brain
regions relevant to Parkinson's Disease based on local field potential data
collected from the brain of marmoset monkeys. Parkinson's disease is a
neurodegenerative disorder, linked to the death of dopaminergic neurons at the
substantia nigra pars compacta, which affects the normal dynamics of the basal
ganglia-thalamus-cortex neuronal circuit of the brain. Although there are
multiple mechanisms underlying the disease, a complete description of those
mechanisms and molecular pathogenesis are still missing, and there is still no
cure. To address this gap, computational models that resemble neurobiological
aspects found in animal models have been proposed. In our model, we performed a
data-driven approach in which a set of biologically constrained parameters is
optimised using differential evolution. Evolved models successfully resembled
single-neuron mean firing rates and spectral signatures of local field
potentials from healthy and parkinsonian marmoset brain data. As far as we are
concerned, this is the first computational model of Parkinson's Disease based
on simultaneous electrophysiological recordings from seven brain regions of
Marmoset monkeys. Results show that the proposed model could facilitate the
investigation of the mechanisms of PD and support the development of techniques
that can indicate new therapies. It can also be applied to other
computational neuroscience studies.
  We make three primary contributions. First, we propose a computational model
of Parkinson's Disease based on simultaneous electrophysiological recordings
from seven brain regions of Marmoset monkeys. Second, we use a novel
data-driven approach in which a set of biologically constrained parameters is
optimised using differential evolution. Third, we release this model under an
open-source license, making it available to the scientific community, to
facilitate further investigation of the mechanisms of PD and the development
of techniques that could indicate new therapies.

speech. This paper reports the evaluations and comparisons of our models for the

evaluate it on the test sets provided by the challenge. The DPCRN model achieves
a significantly higher MOS score (3.57) than the CRN model does. We also find

an approach to improving
the representation of convection in weather and climate models. This is an
attractive framework as it is fundamentally dynamical, removing some of the
assumptions of mass-flux convection schemes which are invalid at current model
resolutions. However, it is still not understood how best to close the
multi-fluid equations for atmospheric convection. In this paper we develop a
simple two-fluid, single-column model with one rising and one falling fluid. No
further modelling of sub-filter variability is included. We then apply this
model to Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, showing that, with minimal closures,
the correct scaling of the heat flux (Nu) is predicted over six orders of
magnitude of buoyancy forcing (Ra). This suggests that even a very simple
two-fluid model can accurately capture the dominant coherent overturning
structures of convection.
  In subsequent experiments to more closely mimic atmospheric convection, we
find that if we initialise strong horizontal gradients of temperature and
moisture into the model, the resulting fluxes and structure of the convection
are poorly predicted. This suggests that any one-parameter closures for, for
example, the eddy diffusivity or momentum flux, will yield realistic results
for the particular value of that parameter, but then be unable to predict the
subsequent evolution of the convection in a realistic way. Realistic evolution
is only achieved if the winds generate their own large-scale rotation, as in
our fully-resolving numerical convection models.
  Finally, we propose a new closure based on the interaction between the rising
and falling fluids, and show that it predicts realistic winds and rotation in
a rotating layer. Further work is needed to fully test and justify this
closure, but it shows promise for multi-fluid convection models.
  In conclusion, simple two-fluid models have potential for the representation
of convection in weather and climate models, but further work is needed to
develop robust closures for the variables required by the model. This is an
important task as single-column models are a testing ground for understanding
the interactions between convection and large-scale flow in global models,
which are still lacking in a realistic way.

CMS) detector is one of two general-purpose
detectors that measure the products of high energy particle interactions in the
Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. The silicon pixel detector is the
innermost component of the CMS tracking system. The detector which was in
operation between 2009 and 2016 has now been replaced with an upgraded one in
the beginning of 2017. During the previous shutdown period of the LHC, a
prototype readout system and a third disk was inserted into the old forward
pixel detector with eight prototype blades constructed using the new digital
read-out chips. Testing the performance of these pilot modules enabled us to
gain operational experience with the upgraded detector. In this paper, the
reconstruction and analysis of the data taken with the new modules are
presented including information on the calibration of the reconstruction
software. The hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual distributions are
also shown.
  Based on 4 pb$^{-1}$ of data collected during 2015 and 2016 proton-proton
collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, the hit efficiency for hits
reconstructed correctly is shown to be independent of track $p_{T}$ and
etmiss. A re-analysis of data from 2012 (81 pb$^{-1}$, collisions at 8 TeV)
has also been performed to check the long-term stability of the system and to
verify that the established standards of precision CMS physics measurements
could be maintained at 13 TeV. The stability of the hit efficiency with
reconstructed $p_T$ and extrapolation of this to 13 TeV is also shown.
Finally, the impact of the new reconstruction algorithms and standards for
the hit efficiency is examined through the measurement of the $B^0_s$ meson
decay rate.
  In all cases the expected compatibility with previous CMS
measurements$^{1-3}$ is observed.

Twitter provides organizations and
individuals an effective way to monitor public emotions towards them and their
competitors. As a result, sentiment analysis has become an important and
challenging task. In this work, we have collected seven publicly available and
manually annotated twitter sentiment datasets. We create a new training and
testing dataset from the collected datasets. We develop an LSTM model to
classify sentiment of a tweet and evaluate the model with the new dataset.
Our experimental results show that the model yields 88% accuracy, 81% precision,
80% recall, and 77% F1-score on the new testing dataset. Our model outperforms
existing models when evaluated on the new dataset and the ISRC dataset.
Finally, our collected dataset is publicly available for sentiment analysis
research and development.

However, building a chat system is not scalable since it often requires a
considerable volume of human-human dialogue data, especially when enforcing
features such as persona, style, or safety. In this work, we study the
challenge of imposing roles on open-domain dialogue systems, with the goal of
making the systems maintain consistent roles while conversing naturally with
humans. To accomplish this, the system must satisfy a role specification that
includes certain conditions on the stated features as well as a system policy
on whether or not certain types of utterances are allowed. For this, we propose
an efficient data collection framework leveraging in-context few-shot learning
of large-scale language models for building role-satisfying dialogue dataset
from scratch. We then compare various architectures for open-domain dialogue
systems in terms of meeting role specifications while maintaining
conversational abilities. Automatic and human evaluations show that our models
effectively maintain roles while engaging in natural conversations. Reproducible
code is available at https://github.com/Shu-ai-team/Role-Conforming-Domain.

the role-playing dialogue task's effectiveness in evaluation, several models are
built and evaluated on the challenging situations induced by the datasets.
Automatic and human evaluations show that the task and datasets are useful in

The efficacies of pesticide
treatments are often evaluated by analyzing the average treatment effects and
risks. The stochastic efficiency with respect to a function is often employed
in such evaluations through ranking the certainty equivalents of each
treatment. The main challenge of using this method is gathering an adequate
number of observations to produce results with statistical power. However, in
many cases, only a limited number of trials are replicated in field
experiments, leaving an inadequate number of observations. In addition, this
method focuses only on the farmer's profit without incorporating the impact of
disease pressure on yield and profit. The objective of our study is to propose
a methodology to address the issue of an insufficient number of observations
using simulations and take into account the effect of disease pressure on yield
through a quantile regression model. We apply this method to the case of
strawberry disease management in Florida.
  The results show that the proposed methodology is practical and provides
farmer-beneficial information beyond just the stochastic efficiency rankings.
It adds perspective to the strategic use of pesticides by highlighting the
probability of obtaining yields and profits at or above those of the
control treatment. Farmers can use this information to tailor pesticide
treatments to the level of disease pressure and consider the risks and
certainty equivalents of different treatment options. Furthermore, the
quantile regression model allows us to understand how the disease pressure
affects the distribution of yields across different quantiles of the control
treatment distribution.
  Farmers, extension agents, and researchers can use the proposed methodology
to discuss management options for strategic disease management and
effectively evaluate pesticide treatments despite the lack of replicated
trials in field experiments. The approach can be applied to any field
experiment with a control treatment and can be used in conjunction with other
methods evaluating pesticide efficacy.

prediction is indispensable. In existing viewport prediction methods, they

turn the attention of the user to specific regions in the video with high
probability. Such information can be included in video subtitles, especially
the one in 360-degree virtual tourism videos. This fact reveals the potential
correlation between navigation information in video subtitles and viewport
trajectory. This correlation provides a strong evidence to support the
navigation-based viewport prediction. In fact, the navigation information can
turn the attention of the user to specific destinations with high probability.
Therefore, we propose a novel viewport prediction method named Nav360 for 360
degree virtual tourism videos, which is driven by navigation information in
video subtitles. This type of prediction is different from traditional
viewport prediction and has several advantages. Namely, the navigation-based
viewport prediction does not need to track the head movement trajectory of the
user and analyze the video saliency. Moreover, it is applicable to any 360
degree virtual tourism video, regardless of the genre and production company,
as long as it contains navigation information in video subtitles. To evaluate
the performance of Nav360, we collect eight 360 degree virtual tourism videos
and implement it in a custom-built dataset. Experimental results show that
Nav360 produces higher prediction accuracy compared to state-of-the-art
viewport prediction methods, especially at long viewing time. Besides, the
bandwidth consumption of Nav360 is compared with that of state-of-the-art
viewport prediction methods, indicating Nav360 has great potential in saving
bandwidth consumption, especially at long viewing time.

role of the Web as a driver of polarization. In order to further our
understanding of the factors behind online polarization, in the present work we
collect and analyze Web browsing histories of tens of thousands of users
alongside careful measurements of the time spent browsing various news sources.
We show that online news consumption follows a polarized pattern, where users'
visits to news sources aligned with their own political leaning are
substantially longer than their visits to other news sources. Next, we show
that such preferences hold at the individual as well as the population level,
as evidenced by the emergence of clear partisan communities of news domains
from aggregated browsing patterns. Finally, we tackle the important question of
the role of user choices in polarization. Are users simply following the links
proffered by their Web environment, or do they exacerbate partisan polarization
by intentionally pursuing like-minded news sources? To answer this question, we
compare browsing patterns with the underlying hyperlink structure spanned by
the considered news domains, finding strong evidence of polarization in
partisan browsing habits beyond that which can be explained by the hyperlink
structure of the Web.
  In particular, our analysis reveals a clearly bipartite hyperlink structure
among news domains, both in terms of the link direction and the social equity
of the resulting pattern. This bipartiteness is strongly correlated with the
geographic equity -- or lack thereof - of the aggregated browsing patterns. As
such, our work demonstrates the inextricability of considerations of
information inequality and partiality in the study of online news consumption
and polarization.
  Finally, as a preliminary contribution, we release the news domain hyperlink
graph we collected in this work. This dataset may be of interest to researchers
studying polarization, as well as those following up on recent
information-theoretic work on measuring inequality in the Web.

with careful measures of time spent browsing various news domains, and demonstrate
the existence of a strongly bipartite hyperlink structure among news domains,

such, our work demonstrates the inextricability of considerations of

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner usually identifies edges first and subsequently fills in
the segmentation mask. Motivated by these observations, we propose a
plug-and-play module, dubbed Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), that can be used with
existing encoder-decoder architectures to process both edge and texture
information. The EG-CNN learns to emphasize the edges in the encoder, to
predict crisp boundaries by an auxiliary edge supervision, and to fuse its
output with the original CNN output. We evaluate the effectiveness of the
EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available datasets, BraTS
19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation. We demonstrate
how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation accuracy and
generalization performance.

very challenging to find unbiased datasets, as biases are often invisible and
models with different parameters and structures may have different biases.

definition. Then we propose MediBB, a novel medical image bias base containing

precise bias mapping MediBNet among multiple sources. Experiments show that

four-layer Aurivillius
compound Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO) at high hydrostatic pressure conditions.
The high-pressure XRD data does not explicitly show structural phase
transitions with hydrostatic pressure, however the observed changes in lattice
parameters indicate structural modifications at different pressure values. In
the initial pressure region values, the lattice parameters $\textit{a}$- and
$\textit{b}$- are nearly equal implying a quasi-tetragonal structure, however
as the pressure increases $\textit{a}$- and $\textit{b}$- diverges apart and
exhibits complete orthorhombic phase at pressure values of about $\geq$8 GPa.
Principal component analysis of high pressure Raman measurements point out an
evident change in the local structure at about 5.5 GPa indicating that the
evolution of the local structure under applied pressure seems to not follow
crystallographic changes (long range order). Nuclear forward scattering (NFS)
measurement reveal the development of magnetic ordering in BFTO at 5K with high
pressures. A progressive increase in magnetic order is observed with increase
in pressure at 5K. Further, NFS measurements carried out at constant pressure
(6.4GPa) and different temperatures indicate that the developed magnetism
disappears at 50K. The applied pressure induced partial replacement of Fe$^{3+}$
by Ti$^{4+}$ may be the reason behind the changes in lattice parameters as
well as appearance of magnetic order in this compound.
  Finally, we note that BFSO and BFTO both exhibit pressure induced partial
replacement of Fe$^{3+}$ by its corresponding companion anion oxide, however the
latter also exhibits appearance of magnetism at high pressure conditions. It is
interesting to investigate if applied pressure can induce only the partial
replacement of Fe$^{3+}$ by Ti$^{4+}$ in other members of this family of
compounds.

expanding universe is studied using
approximate analytic, and exact numerical solution of self-similar equations.
Both solutions have similar properties, which change qualitatively, depending
on the adiabatic powers $\gamma$. In the interval $1<\gamma<\gamma_{cr} \sim
1.16$ analytic and numeric solutions fill all the space without any voids and
they are rather close to each other. At larger $\gamma>\gamma_{cr}$ a pressure
becomes zero at finite radius, and a spherical void appears around the origin
in both solutions. All matter is collected in thin layer behind the shock wave
front. The structure of this layer qualitatively depends on $\gamma$. At the
inner edge of the layer the pressure is always zero, but the density on this
edge is jumping from zero to infinity at $\gamma \approx 1.4$ in both
solutions.
  Both solutions also have the common upper bound of the self-similar regime,
which is smaller for larger $\gamma$. In the case of very strong shocks and
mild adiabatic indices ($\gamma > \gamma_{cr}$) the precursor with the
non-self-similar structure appears in front of the forward edge of the matter
layer. The behavior of the field equations in this subsonic but non-self-
similar precursor explains the typical features of the corresponding graphic
lines in the shocks problems: the presence of the maximum in the density at
finite distance in front of the shock wave front, the presence of the minimum
in the density at finite distance behind the shock wave front, and the non-
monotonicity of the density profile behind the shock wave front.
  Finally, the structure of the layers behind the strong adiabatic and
convection shocks is discussed in terms of the characteristic approach. It is
shown that the structure of the layer behind the adiabatic shock is generally
the same as in the self-similar case, while the convection shock always changes
into the rarefaction wave or a convection fan, and the picture behind the
convection shock is significantly different from the self-similar one.
  In conclusion, the main features of the strong shock wave propagation in the
expanding universe are discussed in terms of the characteristic approach, which
gives a general qualitative picture of the shock structure and provides a
basis for analysis of all particular cases.
