a regime of macroscopic quantum tunneling to one of phase diffusion as a
function of temperature, where the transition temperature $T^{*}$ is
gate-tunable. The switching probability distributions are shown to be
consistent with a small shunt capacitance and moderate damping, resulting in a
switching current which is a small fraction of the critical current. Phase
locking between two JJs leads to a difference in switching current between that
of a JJ measured in isolation and that of the same JJ measured in an asymmetric
SQUID loop. In the case of the loop, $T^*$ is also tuned by a magnetic flux.
Switching current is tuned by magnetic flux in the loop and is dependent on
the geometry of the loop. Our results suggest that that InAs JJs and SQUIDs can
be tuned to produce a strong thermal noise component in the DC critical current,
making them useful for applications which require a noise-tunable JJ or SQUID.
Moreover, the fact that $T^*$ can be tuned by a gate or magnetic flux implies
that these devices can be used as switches with a well-controlled switching
voltage.

SQUID-magnetic-flux-induced deterministic switching, defined by a large
magnetic flux dependence of the switching current, prior to the onset of
diffusion. This regime ends in a second crossover temperature $T^{**}$. The
physical basis of this second crossover is not clear.

including its architecture, design choices and implementation details. We
evaluate the performance of s4cmb in different configurations through
benchmarking tests against the time required to simulate a data set of
reasonable size with various levels of instrumental systematics, and against
the ability of the package to produce realistic raw data streams and
instrumental systematics effects. Finally, we mention some of the future

the two ends of a randomly selected edge are independent. In the paper, we take
one step further and consider ensembles of LDPC codes with degree-degree
correlations. For this, we propose two methods to construct an ensemble of
degree-degree correlated LDPC codes. We then derive a system of density
evolution equations for such degree-degree correlated LDPC codes over a binary
erasure channel (BEC). By conducting extensive numerical experiments, we show
how the degree-degree correlation affects the performance of LDPC codes. Our
numerical results show that LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlation
could improve the maximum tolerable erasure probability. Moreover, increasing
the negative degree-degree correlation could lead to better unequal error
protection (UEP) design.

detection, and single photon detection, to the widely used vacuum+weak decoy

proposal reveals that partial phase randomization is not sufficient to
guarantee the security of phase-encoding QKD systems with weak coherent states.

can be implemented by only adding an optical phase shift in one of the long

information about the phase randomization of the source. Furthermore, the
feasibility of the attack can be implemented in practice is discussed.

implemented as a smart contract and at its peak one of the largest consumers of

all of its transactions visible on the blockchain. We take advantage of this
unprecedented transparency to gain insight into the mechanics, impact on
participants, and evolution of Forsage.

claims of trustworthiness and profitability, and how Forsage activity is

expose and understand scams, and to provide context to regulations around
cryptocurrencies.
  Finally, our work highlights the challenge that schemes like Forsage pose to
cryptocurrency anonymity goals. Sectors of the industry that prioritize
anonymity should consider how their technologies can be used to perpetuate

first-principle tight-binding (TB) models. The standard way of describing
optical properties is the velocity gauge, defined by linear coupling to the
vector potential.
  In finite systems a transformation to represent the electromagnetic radiation
by the electric field instead is possible, albeit subtleties arise in periodic
systems. The resulting dipole gauge is a multi-orbital generalization of
Peierl's substitution. In this work, we investigate accuracy of both pathways,
with particular emphasis on gauge invariance, for TB models constructed from
maximally localized Wannier functions. Focusing on paradigmatic two-dimensional
materials, we construct first-principle models and calculate the response to
electromagnetic fields in linear response and for strong excitations.
Benchmarks against fully converged first-principle calculations allow for
ascertaining the accuracy of the TB models. We find that the dipole gauge
provides a more accurate description than the velocity gauge in all cases. The
main deficiency of the velocity gauge is an imperfect cancellation of
paramagnetic and diamagnetic current. Formulating a corresponding sum rule
however provides a way to explicitly enforce this cancellation. This procedure
corrects the TB models in the velocity gauge, yielding excellent agreement with
dipole gauge and thus gauge invariance.
  Our results provide TB models that can be used to study optical and
thermalelectric properties, as well as electro- and thermomechanical ones, of
any solid-state system within a first-principle framework. It also yields a
method to assess the accuracy of any TB model, regardless of the application.
Finally, it opens the possibility to investigate gauge-dependent phenomena,
e.g., the dynamical gauge field coupling to fermions.
  We hope that this work will further stimulate the development of more
efficient methods to construct TB models and will help to clarify the
formalism when it is used.
  Last, we provide a concise guide on how to define first-principle TB models
of optical, electro- and thermomechanical properties.
  In the Appendices, we provide further details on the different pathways to
define first-principle TB models, test the accuracy of the various methods,
and discuss the relation between our formalism and others.

obtained from telemetry, and resource selection functions (RSF) are used for
inference. Another important focus of wildlife research is estimation and
modeling population size and density. Recently developed spatial
capture-recapture (SCR) models accomplish this objective using individual
encounter history data with auxiliary spatial information on location of
capture. SCR models include encounter probability functions that are
intuitively related to RSFs, but to date, no one has extended SCR models to
allow for explicit inference about space usage and resource selection. We
develop a statistical framework for jointly modeling space usage, resource
selection, and population density by integrating SCR data, such as from camera
traps, mist-nets, or conventional catch-traps, with resource selection data
from telemetered individuals. We provide a framework for estimation based on
marginal likelihood, wherein we estimate simultaneously the parameters of the
SCR and RSF models.
  Our method leads to increases in precision for estimating population density
and parameters of ordinary SCR models. Importantly, we also find that SCR
models alone can estimate parameters of resource selection functions and, as
such, SCR methods can be used as the sole source for studying space-usage;
however, precision will be higher when telemetry data are available. Finally,
we find that SCR models will tend to over-estimate density in areas with
resources that are more attractive than the average resource in the population
and underestimate density in areas with resources that are less attractive
than the average resource in the population, thus SCR/SCR model comparisons
will be useful for studying patchiness and aggregation in populations.
  In conclusion, we urge researchers to report all data sources available for
their study subject and consider SCR as the primary method for estimating
population density. We also recommend SCR/SCR model comparisons to infer
information about space-usage and resource selection and to use telemetry
data to estimate parameters of resource selection functions with higher precision.
Finally, we provide a framework for statisticians to perform complex
aggregation inference in SCR models and researchers studying space-usage to
assess the relative attractiveness of different resources.

studying political polarization in political and social systems. Several
methods are used commonly to measure polarization in social networks by purely
inspecting their structure. We analyse eight of such methods and show that all
of them yield high polarization scores even for random networks with similar
density and degree distributions to typical real-world networks. Further, some
of the methods are sensitive to degree distributions and relative sizes of the
polarized groups. We propose normalization to the existing scores and a minimal
set of tests that a score should pass in order for it to be suitable for
separating polarized networks from random noise. The performance of the scores
increased by 38%-220% after normalization in a classification task of 203
networks. Further, we find that the choice of method is not as important as
normalization, and it's the effort of centering the scores around 0.5 to be 3
times more important than the change in methodology. This work opens up the
possibility of investigating the effect of normalization on other statistical
properties and may lead to a re-evaluation of existing research on
decomposition of polarization in complex systems.

program termination. The algorithm and this theory are intended to be

under the ultrastrong coupling regime. Parity symmetry of Rabi model only
permits the super-Rabi oscillations with periodic generation of even photons in
cavity, which is realized by the laser driven flip of qubit and the parity
conserved transitions induced by Rabi interaction. Combined with dissipation,

ultrastrong coupling regime and cavity with dissipation, which may be
useful for exploring quantum phase transition and nonlinear transmutation in
cavity QED.

dynamical quantum phase transition in open Rabi superócoid model. The
transition is a result of an competition between an effective magnetic field
and Rabi coupling, which can be controlled by a parameter of driving
frequency. When transition occurs, even photons will accumulate in cavity with
the increase of parameter, and then bundle emission happens immediately when
cavity is filled with quanta. Also, we find that bundle emission can also be
induced by a monochromatic laser in the context of two-qubit dipole-dipole
interaction under certain symmetry, which may be realized in semiconductor
microtraps.

network (of unknown size) under the presence of a large number of Byzantine

complete knowledge about the entire state of the network at every round

  Our main contribution is a randomized distributed algorithm that estimates
the size of a network under the presence of a large number of Byzantine nodes.
In particular, our algorithm estimates the size of a sparse, "small-world",
expander network with up to $O(n^{1 - \delta})$ Byzantine nodes, where $n$ is
the (unknown) network size and $\delta$ can be be any arbitrarily small (but
fixed) positive constant. Our algorithm outputs a (fixed) constant factor
estimate of $\log(n)$ with high probability; the correct estimate of the
network size will be known to a large fraction ($(1 - \epsilon)$-fraction, for
any fixed positive constant $\epsilon$) of the honest nodes. Our algorithm is
fully distributed, lightweight, and simple to implement, runs in $O(\log^3{n})$
rounds, and requires nodes to send and receive messages of only small-sized
messages per round; any node's local computation cost per round is also small.
To our knowledge, our algorithm is the first to achieve even a sublinear
roundbound for a problem as fundamental as network size estimation in the full
information model under presence of Byzantine nodes.
  We believe that our algorithm will be of interest to many problems in
Network Science, Social Network Analysis, and Complex Systems; also, our
techniques may be useful to many problems in Distributed Computation, Byzantine
Rendezvous Problems, and Consensus problems, which need to be executed in
networks prone to malicious behavior.

effect in magnetic materials with
vanishing magnetization has renewed interest in understanding and engineering
this phenomenon. Antiferromagnetic antiperovskites are one of emerging material
classes that exhibit a variety of interesting properties owing to a complex
electronic band structure and magnetic ordering. Reports on the anomalous
Nernst effect and its magnitude in this class of materials are, however, very
limited. This scarcity may be partly due to the experimental difficulty of
reliably quantifying the anomalous Nernst coefficient. Here, we report
experiments on the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite
Mn$_3$NiN thin films. Measurement of both the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects
using the same sample and measurement geometry makes it possible to directly
compare these two effects and quantify the anomalous Nernst coefficient and
conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN. We carefully evaluate the spatial distribution of
the thermal gradient in the sample and use finite element modeling to
corroborate our experimental results.
  The anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN thin films are
found to be significantly larger than previously reported in the same material
type. Furthermore, the anomalous Nernst coefficient is shown to be
insensitively dependent on the magnetic field direction making it possible to
extract this quantity for various Nernst field orientations. By comparing the
measured anomalous Nernst effect to the sum of the ordinary Nernst effect and a
rotation of the anomalous thermal transport coefficient with the magnetization,
we demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst effect is purely magnetization
rotational in nature (no spin-oral coupling) and all the contribution to the
anomalous Nernst coefficient comes from the individual Hall and thermal
conductivity channels. Lastly, the anomalous Nernst coefficient is found to be
linearly dependent on the electronic carrier density, which helps to understand
its origin and possible spin-orbit coupling in this material type.
  Finally, we discuss the theoretical model that describes the anomalous Nernst
effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites and propose several experiments to
further investigate this phenomenon in Mn$_3$NiN.

solution to
non-autonomous obstacle problems of the form
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\},
  \end{equation*} where the function $f$ satisfies $p-$growth conditions with
respect to the gradient variable, for $1<p<2$, and $\mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)$
is the class of admissible functions. Here we show that, if the obstacle $\psi$
is bounded, then a Sobolev regularity assumption on the gradient of the
obstacle $\psi$ transfers to the gradient of the solution, provided the partial
map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a Sobolev space, $W^{1, p+2}$. The
novelty here is that we deal with subquadratic growth conditions with respect
to the gradient variable, i.e. $f(x, \xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ with $1<p<2,$ and
where the map $a$ belongs to a Sobolev space.
  Finally, if the map $a$ is bounded then a Holder continuity result for the
solution is established.
  In the case the obstacle $\psi$ is not bounded we prove a higher
differentiability result provided the obstacle $\psi$ has a bounded gradient.
Finally, if the map $f$ is convex with respect to $x$ then a new result about
the regularity of the weak solution is established.
  In the last part of the paper we provide some applications to the theory of
non-local obstacle problems.

the leading astronomical research institutes in the world. When van Rhijn took
over at the retirement of Kapteyn, it was in the process of coordinating
Kapteyn's Plan of Selected Areas. Van Rhijn's research was solid and
professional work, but in his papers he invariably stopped before discussing
how his findings did fit into the larger scheme of things. He maybe was
unimaginative but it did lack the link to the larger view towards the emerging
picture of the structure of the Galaxy. Van Rhijn was unfortunate to be
hampered throughout almost his complete directorate by factors, that severely
limited his attempts to obtain more funding in spite of local support by his
university. These were of course in the first place the Great Depression of the
1930s and the Second World War and its aftermath, while during most of the
1940s he suffered from tuberculosis. But also the remote location of Groningen
compared to Leiden, where a major infrastructure led by three important
protegees of Kapteyn was in place, and the governmental bias towards support
for Leiden over Groningen was an important factor. Finally I examine van
Rhijn's management style and his relations towards his small staff, which he
demanded to be independent in their research and yet at the same time wanted
them to work towards a coordinated overall programme towards the coordination
of the Selected Areas programme. Conclusively I speculate on the reasons for
van Rhijn's relative obscurity in the face of his important contributions to
aerial photography and its use in astronomical research.

1972. The HCS program built upon the foundation laid by van Rhijn's Selected
Areas project and it did bridge the gap towards the digital era. It was a
practical example of how van Rhijn's work did contribute towards the larger
picture

the approximate solution with respect to the optimal control with known
dynamics. We show that the longer the trial or the more side information is

F-16 aircraft simulator and MuJoCo's environments illustrate that, despite the
scarcity of data, the algorithm can provide performance comparable to
reinforcement learning algorithms trained over millions of environment
interactions. Besides, we show that the algorithm outperforms existing
techniques combining system identification and model predictive control.

theoretical analysis, which also achieves competitive performance. As a
highlight, we design and control a robotic system (Quadcopter) to achieve a
complex task (follow a pipe) using only a simple gravity model and no

different demographic groups. Student learning data is collected from 70 online
learning modules assigned as both online homework and self-study material in
both Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters, with the first 41 modules being
assigned before campus closure in Spring 2020. Students' ability to stay on
track is measured by three data indicators: percentage of modules submitted
before the due date, percentage of modules submitted early for extra credit,
and percentage of modules properly engaged with. The student population is
divided into two demographic groups according to each of the four demographic
variables: Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status and First generation status. All
three data indicators from both semesters are first compared between each pair
of demographic groups within the same semester, and then compared within the
same group between the two semesters. Exam and course scores are also compared
between demographics groups in Fall 2020 and against scores from the Fall 2019
semester. The analysis revealed that remote learning significantly reduced
on-time and early submission for first-generation students, but increased the
frequency of early submission for transfer students. Under-represented minority
students had higher percentage of engaged modules during the pandemic, while
non-URM students had a sharper decrease. Women had higher percentage of on-time
submission than men during the pandemic, while men had a sharper decrease. All
student demographics generally caught up in terms of submission and engagement
performance when campus reopened in Spring 2020. This suggests that some of
the effects of remote learning on students' ability to keep up with the pace of
instruction may be temporary.
  The implications of this study are that instructors should be aware of the
potential heterogeneous impact of remote learning and adjust assignments and
instructional strategies accordingly to benefit historically under-represented
groups. Additionally online homework and engagement modules should be tested and
validated before large-scale implementation, especially during a pandemic when
student learning environment is drastically changed.
  Finally, the study suggests that both theoretical and empirical approaches in
physics education research should reconsider the concept of "learning loss" in
the context of remote learning, and how it relates to students' ability to
keep up with the pace of instruction.

in a four-valued paracomplete and
paradoxical logic, that is, a logic in which propositions are neither true nor
false, but can be both true and false, and propositions are also inconsistent.
This approach to set theory, L0, avoids the need for axioms such as the
foundation axiom and the axiom of choice, as they follow from the rules of the
logic. Furthermore, in this framework, Russell's paradox, rather than
leading to a contradiction, reveals a fault in the naming convention that we
propose to resolve by adding a suffix to each name to indicate the set to which
it belongs. We then explore some of the consequences of this approach to set
theory, including a discussion of the Cantor-Bernstein theorem and the
Hausdorff paradox.
  We also examine the relationship between L0 and other systems of set theory
including ZFC (Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice). We argue
that ZFC is an ontology (a theory of existence) whereas L0 is an axiomatic
system that defines a particular ontology, and as such, there is no deep
relationship between them. Finally, we address the question of why a
four-valued paracomplete and paradoxical logic is necessary to realise the
sets that are commonly accepted by mathematicians. We argue that the answer
lies in the notion of equivalence classes.

cloud and on-premise HPC systems offer similar computational resources, their
network architecture and performance may differ significantly. For example,
these systems use fundamentally different network transport and routing
protocols, which may introduce network noise that can eventually limit the
application scaling. This work analyzes network performance, scalability, and
cost of running HPC workloads on cloud systems. First, we consider latency,
bandwidth, and collective communication patterns in detailed small-scale
measurements, and then we simulate network performance at a larger scale. We
validate our approach on four popular cloud providers and three on-premise HPC
systems, showing that network (and also OS) noise can significantly impact
performance and cost both at small and large scale.

network performance measurements and proportional scaling up to 8192 nodes.
Deploying an application involves choosing the target hardware nodes to fit
the MPI communicator structure. Our understanding of network performance allows
to predict communication patterns and cost across different cloud providers
and HPC systems. We show that network performance is the main factor in
optimizing deployment cost, and our approach can reduce cost up to 30% in some
cloud deployments. Finally, our predictions can steer deployment decisions by
avoiding under or over-provisioning. With our approach, if the prediction
failure occurs, it is usually noticeable early in the deployment (during the
initialization of the first processes), allowing for quick intervention to
optimize the deployment.

application developers/porters by detailing the network performance,
scalability, and deployment considerations across on-premise HPC systems and

has many practical applications. Recently, this setup gained a lot of interest
in applications over wireless where communication constraints can be a
performance bottleneck, especially when the contexts come from a large
$d$-dimensional space. In this paper, we consider adaptive linear bandits where
the contexts are adaptive and may come from a large Euclidean space. We
derivative a communication-efficient algorithm, called ComAdaptUCB, for this
model and prove that it achieves a regret bound of
$\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{dK\log(K)}\right)$ where $K$ is the number of rounds. This
bound improves upon the existing bound of $\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$
for the non-communication-constrained adaptive linear bandit. We also prove that
ComAdaptUCB is communication-optimal, in the sense that there exists a lower
bound of $\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ on the regret of any
communication-constrained algorithm. ComAdaptUCB is simple to implement, has a
linear space complexity, and can handle unbounded contexts. ComAdaptUCB is
made of two phases per arm: exploration and exploitation. In the exploration
phase, the algorithm asks for the context from the arm, runs a local learning
algorithm (UCB) for some specific contexts, and then approximates the arm's
parameter using the learned parameters from the contexts sampled in the
interaction. The approximation is via least-squares. The learned parameters are
shared across arms to reduce communication. The approximation error is bound
using matrix norms, which leads to ComAdaptUCB's improved regret bound. To
illustrate the communication reduction, let's assume that contexts are $\mathcal
{R}^d$, e.g., images. Suppose we have $B$ arms and, per round, we ask for the
context from the selected arm. If we use plain UCB, we need to communicate the
context to the learner $BK$ times. With ComAdaptUCB, we only need to ask for
the context $K$ times (plus few more communications to achieve the same bound)
and we still get the same bound, which is a significant reduction in
communication, especially when $B\gg 1$.

network theory, this work studies the extremal gain of optimal power control
over binary (on/off) power control, especially in large interference networks,
in search of new theoretical insights. Whereas numerical studies have already
established that in practice binary power control is quite close to optimal,
extremal analysis considers the extremal (worst or best) possible sum rate
over the random channel realizations under power control and binary control,
and compares them with the worst and best possible sum rates under binary
control. For two-user interference channels, it is shown that the worst possible
sum rate under binary control is greater than the worst possible sum rate under
power control, while the best possible sum rate under binary control is
proportional to that under power control. For general wireless networks, it is
shown that the extremal (worst or best) sum rate under power control is
proportional to the extremal sum rate under binary control, which implies that
also in terms of extremal performance, binary power control is close to optimal.
In addition, it is shown that the range of the ratio of the extremal sum rates
under power and binary controls is $[0,1]$, which numerically verifies that for
all channel realizations, the sum rate under power control is not less than
that under binary control. Numerical examples are provided to illustrate the
theoretical results.

robo-physics problem since the uncertainty in terrain dynamics introduced by
ground deformation complicates the dynamical modelling and control methods.
Moreover, learning how (e.g. what controls and mechanisms) to move efficiently
and stably on soft ground is a bigger issue. This work seeks to control a 1D
monopod hopper to jump to desired height. To achieve this goal, I first set up
and validate a discrete element method (DEM) based soft ground simulation
environment of a spherical granular material. With this simulation environment,
I generate resistive force theory (RFT) based models of the ground reaction
force. Then I use the RFT model to develop a feedforward force control for this
robot. In the DEM simulation, I use feedback control to compensate for
variations in the ground reaction force from the RFT model predictions and
achieve better performance. I also use the feedback control to study three
different tuning strategies. This study shows that the feedback control is
necessary to achieve desirable performance, and it also shows possible benefits
and drawbacks of each of the tuning methods.

controlling and studying the interaction of a robotic system with a DEM simulation
of a granular material (i.e. the ground). This set of methods is generally
applicable to any robo-physics simulation and can be beneficial for
industrial simulation of systems on soft ground or for research purposes when
studying ground interaction.
  I also release the DEM simulation environment and the robot urdf as a
contribution to the scientific community, to facilitate further simulations and
real world experiments.
  Throughout this work, I explain the following components: the 1D hopper
design, the DEM simulation environment, the RFT model, and the control
strategies. Therefore, this work is also a tutorial on these topics.

2022.

retrieval. This new computational model is an extension of the word-embedding
approach called FastText, and is called FastHier. We show that this new
computational model is effective at retrieving documents that contain phrases
and sentences relevant to search queries. We introduce a new algorithm to
learn this computational model, called Dual-Limited-Bounded Method (DLBM). This
new algorithm is an extension of the limited-bounded method for training
deep-neural-networks, and is inspired by the way humans search for documents
and relate search results to search queries. We compare several existing
computational models with the proposed model, and show through search tasks
over three medium size data-sets that DLBM outperforms the existing approaches
by up to 31% in terms of precision and by up to 25% in terms of recall.
Furthermore, the proposed model is shown to outperform the existing approaches
in terms of sub-second query-time while supporting search queries over hundreds

consider linkages in information {\em networks} that are increasingly common in
real-world scenarios. Current approaches also tend to present topics as an
abstract probability distribution over words, etc rather than as tangible nodes
from the original network.

quantum system: Annealing explores equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian with
slowly changing parameters and can be exploited as a tool for solving complex
optimization problems. In contrast, quenches are sudden changes of the
Hamiltonian, producing a non-equilibrium situation. Here, we investigate the
relation between the two cases. Specifically, we show that the minimum of the
annealing gap, which is an important bottleneck of quantum annealing
algorithms, can be revealed from a dynamical quench parameter which describes
the dynamical quantum state after the quench. Combined with statistical tools
including the training of a neural network, the relation between quench and
annealing dynamics can be exploited to reproduce the full functional behavior
of the annealing gap from the quench data. We show that the partial or full
knowledge about the annealing gap which can be gained in this way can be used
to design optimized quantum annealing protocols with a practical
time-to-solution benefit. Our results are obtained from simulating random Ising
Hamiltonians, representing hard-to-solve instances of the exact cover problem.
We thus believe that our approach has promising potential to help designing
more efficient quantum annealing algorithms and protocols in general.
  From a theoretical physics point of view our work demonstrates how insights
gained from studying dynamical quantum state after a quench can be used to
investigate equilibrium phases of a quantum system, in this case the different
annealing phases of a quantum annealing protocol. This reverse engineering
approach allows us to systematically map the equilibrium phase diagram of the
quantum annealing protocol, which can be related to any optimization problem
that is being solved. Knowing the equilibrium phases directly may then be used
to design more efficient annealing protocols with a practical time-to-solution
benefit.

  We define infix/postfix alignments and propose approaches to their computation
based on boolean satisfiability solving, algorithmic approaches, and
constraint-based checking. Furthermore, we evaluate these approaches using two
event data sets, one related to the airline industry and another to the
hospitality industry, and analyze the results of the evaluation.
  Our approach based on constraint technology is the most efficient but has the
restriction to only work for loose alignments. Our algorithmic approach is
practical for all three deviation types but less efficient. Still, our studies
show that infix/postfix alignments can be computed in acceptable time for
real-life event data.
  Our proposals are relevant to conformance checking, process deviation
analysis, and process quality checking, in particular, for localized deviation
analysis where process deviations in specific parts of the process need to be
detected, localized, and quantified.

attack vectors like backdoor attacks. Such attacks embed a secret functionality
in a neural network activated when the trigger is added to its input. In most
works in the literature, the trigger is static, both in terms of location and
pattern. The effectiveness of various detection mechanisms depends on this
property. It was recently shown that countermeasures in image classification,
like Neural Cleanse and ABS, could be bypassed with dynamic triggers that are
effective regardless of their pattern and location. Still, such backdoors are
demanding as they require a large percentage of poisoned training data. In this
work, we are the first to show that dynamic backdoor attacks could happen due
to a global average pooling layer without increasing the percentage of the
poisoned training data. Nevertheless, our experiments in sound classification,
text sentiment analysis, and image classification show this to be very
difficult in practice.
  We observe that the weight of a global average pooling layer has a
aggregation effect on the activated features of the upstream layers at each
data sample. These features are sensitive to the input and the model
configuration. The re-activation of the frozen layers except for the last two,
and the discrepancy among different model architectures and training
configurations further support this observation. As a result, the activated
backdoor pattern in the activated features of the pooling layer is
input-dependent, which makes the attack difficult to detect. Our analysis and
experiments show that to counter such attacks, one needs to study the
activation of the backdoor pattern in the features before the pooling layer,
which is feasible but expensive. We also show how the aggregation effect
expands the attack to data beyond the training samples.
  We propose and evaluate detection strategies in sound classification, text
sentiment analysis, and image classification to make such attacks detectable.
We show that our strategies are effective regardless of the dynamic backdoor
trigger pattern and location. We also show how our approaches are superior to
existing countermeasures.
  We believe our findings and strategies are important in developing global
countermeasures against backdoor attacks in deep learning, which is one step
towards making ML as a service trustworthy.
  Finally, we emphasize the necessity of further theoretical works in
understanding the behavior of backdoor attacks and countermeasures in DNNs.

dynamical systems onto their slowest nonresonant spectral submanifolds (SSMs).
We use observed data to locate a low-dimensional, attracting slow SSM and
compute a maximally sparse approximation to the reduced dynamics on it. The
recently released SSMLearn algorithm uses implicit optimization to fit a
spectral submanifold to data and reduce the dynamics to the normal form. Here,
we present two simplified algorithms, which reformulate manifold fitting and
normal form computation as explicit problems under certain assumptions. We show
on several numerical examples that these algorithms are orders of magnitude
faster than the implicit algorithm in SSMLearn while still retaining similar
accuracy in model reduction.
  We also propose a variant of the algorithm that uses recent results in
nonlinear feedback control (NFC) construction. The new algorithm allows us to
derive a feedback control that globally attracts the reduced system to the
selected slow SSM. This is uncommon in data-driven model reduction, where
reduced systems are generally required to be nonresonant locally around a
selected attracting invariant manifold (a SSM or a torus). We show that the
NFC algorithm enables us to globally attract a toroidal SSM, which is
challenging to identify data-dependently. Finally, we show how the NFC algorithm
can be used to globally attract a multi-manifold consisting of several
nonlinear spectral submanifolds.
  Overall, the algorithms presented in this work offer several contributions to
data-driven model reduction. They are faster than the algorithm in
SSMLearn, simpler to implement, and with some additional structure, they also
construct globally attracting slow SSMs and their normal forms.

visible reference spectra. The PFS/MSXO spectrograph on the Anglo-Australian
Telescope provided ~10 Å resolution in a 400-1100 nm spectral range for 10
minute integrations. Although sensitive enough to detect molecular cations in
cometary environments, PFS/MSXO was not optimized for the characterization of
astrophysical molecules and was largely filled with calibration and scientific

understanding optical emission from cometary environments and as a warning

  [Abstract]
  Molecular cations are present in various astronomical environments, most
notably in cometary atmospheres and tails where sunlight produces exceptionally
bright near-UV to visible transitions. Such cations typically have
longer-wavelength and brighter electronic emission than their corresponding
neutrals. A robust understanding of their near-UV to visible properties would
allow these cations to be used as tools for probing the local plasma
environments or as tracers of neutral gas in cometary environments. However,
full spectral models are not possible for characterization of small, oxygen
containing molecular cions given the body of molecular data currently
available.

new approach to traditional
spectroscopy where the spectral cross-correlation with a template spectrum can
be done entirely on-device. By creating photonic devices with a carefully
designed, modulated transmission spectrum, the cross-correlation can be carried
out optically without requiring any dispersion, vastly simplifying the
instrument and reducing its cost. The measured correlation can be used for a
variety of applications, from precise spectral assignment to quantitative
detection of multiple species.
  We demonstrate this technique for the detection of oxygen in a flame. The
spectra are measured using a photonic device with two independent gain sections
and a single mode interference (SMI) sensor. The transmission of the SMI sensor
is modulated in one gain section while the gain is modulated in the other gain
section. The naturally aligned spectral features of oxygen allow for
high-sensitivity detection in this all-device approach, with a limit of
detection of 2.5% by volume. Future device optimizations will allow for the
detection of multiple species and will improve the limit of detection for
high-interest species.
  We also demonstrate a second approach to achieve the same cross-correlation
but instead use a single gain section and two SMI sensors. This approach can
be used when there are not sufficient independent gain sections available. In
this case, the transmission is modulated in one of the SMI sensors while the
gain is modulated in the photonic device. The second SMI sensor is used to
carry out the cross-correlation optically. This approach has been used to
detect carbon dioxide in the exhaust of a combustion engine with a limit of
detection of 1% by volume.
  These approaches show the successful implementation of all-device
spectroscopy and demonstrate its utility for detecting oxygen and carbon dioxide
in various applications.

  Relational machine learning models for drug data analysis often incorporate
relationship information between drugs. This information may be represented by
textual descriptions, binary interaction scores or continuous similarity
metrics. Models may use this information to compute pair-wise interactions or
embed drugs in a continuous space in a way that the distance between them is
proportional to the similarity. Therefore, related learning techniques such as
multi-relational link prediction and relational neural networks become

this domain, we propose a general framework which unifies the mentioned
techniques and provides a transparent comparison of existing model
configurations. Performance metrics and evaluation protocols are also
discussed. Finally, we emphasize important future research directions within this
domain, among them multi-task learning, transfer learning and the integration of
more complex drug structures.

the communication bottleneck between the nodes and the parameter server. A
popular solution in the literature is to allow each node to do several local
updates on the model in each iteration before sending it back to the PS. While
this mitigates the communication bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of
the data owned by the different nodes has proven to delay convergence and bias
the model. In this work, we study random walk (RW) learning algorithms for
tackling the communication and data heterogeneity problems. The main idea is to
leverage available direct connections among the nodes themselves, which are
typically "cheaper" than the communication to the PS. In a random walk, the
model is thought of as a "baton" that is passed from a node to one of its
neighbors after being updated in each iteration. The challenge in designing the
RW is the data heterogeneity and the uncertainty about the distribution of the
data across the nodes. A naive RW would converge to the skills (optimal
parameters) of the nodes themselves rather than the global optimal parameters
that fit the entire dataset. A number of RW algorithms have been proposed to
address this problem [e.g., Federated Averaging (FA) of RW, Meta learning of
RW, etc.]. However, they all assume i.i.d. data within the graph and are
constrained to simple geometric graphs (e.g., regular graphs, expander graphs).
The i.i.d. data assumption is not realistic for many applications (e.g., FL
for healthcare [1], FL for education [2], FL for social networks [3], FL for
energy [4]), where the goal is often to learn a model that is useful for
predicting outcomes between nodes that are directly connected. Even more
importantly, the studies above assume that the graph topology is given and
fixed. Our DW-RW algorithm overcomes the above limitations by designing a
RW algorithm that can learn an optimal graph topology, as well as update the
model to fit the data owned by the nodes, while exploiting the underlying
graph topology for communication.

mostly theoretical topic. In both idealized numerical simulations and

method called Few-Shot Medical Image Segmentation (FSMIS) that utilizes
episodic few-shot learning to segment new classes of medical images when only
a few examples of annotated data are available. FSMIS first creates a base
model through supervised training using a large pool of unlabeled data and
then uses an adaptive protocol to create class-specific few-shot models for
each new class. We also designed a protocol to select the best few shot
predictions by using human expert segmentation ratings in addition to
traditional metric scores (e.g., Jaccard and Dice). Our experiments on the
Kidneyeyeeis and BRATS datasets show that FSMIS significantly outperforms the
baselines and previous approaches that also use few-shot learning. For example,
on the Kidneyeyeeis dataset, FSMIS has about a 10% higher metric score than
the best baseline method that uses classic few-shot learning. We believe that
FSMIS has the potential to segment new classes of medical images that have
never been seen before, even when only a few annotated examples are available.

would open it up to a plethora of applications. However, in this case the

user studies, we observe a clear preference for our avatar model and we
demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on quantitative evaluation metrics.

handling.

representation which can be a stepping stone towards high-fidelity virtual
human assistants that can be deployed in the wild.

understanding how evolving local structural environments dictate performance
and durability. Here, we leverage graph neural networks to define a physically
interpretable metric for local disorder. This metric encodes the diversity of
the local atomic configurations as a continuous spectrum between the solid and
liquid phases, quantified against a distribution of thermal perturbations. We
apply this novel methodology to three prototypical examples with varying levels
of disorder: (1) solid-liquid interfaces, (2) polycrystalline microstructures,
and (3) grain boundaries. Using elemental aluminum as a case study, we show how
our paradigm can track the spatio-temporal evolution of interfaces,
incorporating a mathematically defined description of the spatial boundary
between order and disorder. We further show how to extract physics-preserved
gradients from our continuous disorder fields, which may be used to understand
and predict materials performance and failure. Overall, our framework provides
an intuitive and generalizable pathway to quantify the relationship between
complex local atomic structure and coarse-grained materials phenomena.
Furthermore, our methodology is scalable to high-resolution simulations and
experimental data, making it a powerful tool for the multi-scale study of
materials disorder. Finally, we propose a new paradigm for the analysis of
simulations and experiments, in which the simulation of a perfect crystal is
used as a reference for the calculation of disorder in real materials. This
approach reveals the impact of thermodynamics and kinetics on disorder in
real-systems, highlighting the crucial role of local disorder in understanding
materials phenomena.

understood as a competition between two velocity scales: the speed of
re-aggregation, in which particles relax towards a low-energy configuration
determined by viscous and capillary forces, and the difference of velocity

based on this competition is consistent with the experimental failure patterns.

behaves like a string of clusters of fixed length, with the difference of

making decisions online? Often, the predictive mean is used for this purpose,

predictive distribution can give a measure of the predictive variance and
should be utilized to select the most trustworthy prediction. We propose to
select the prediction at a reliability level $\epsilon \in [0.25, 0.75]$ which
covers $100\epsilon$% of the predictive distribution. We perform experiments on

results show that choosing the predictive percentile covers the true outcome

looked at the implications of rounding continuous random variables, rounding
may be applied to functions of discrete random variables as well. For example,
to infer on suicide excess deaths after a national emergency, authorities may
provide a rounded average of deaths before and after the emergency started.
Suicide rates tend to be relatively low around the world and such rounding may
seriously affect inference on the change of suicide rate. In this paper, we
study the scenario when a rounded to nearest integer average is used to
estimate a non-negative discrete random variable. Specifically, our interest is
in drawing inference on a parameter from the pmf of Y, when we get U = n[Y/n]
as a proxy for Y. The probability generating function of U, E(U), and Var(U)
capture the effect of the coarsening of the support of Y. Also, moments and
estimators of distribution parameters are explored for some special cases. We
show that under certain conditions, there is little impact from rounding.
However, we also find scenarios where rounding can significantly affect
statistical inference as demonstrated in two applications. The simple methods
we propose are able to partially counter rounding error effects.
  In the United States, suicide rates tend to be relatively low compared to
other causes of death. To assess the excess suicide deaths following the
COVID-19 pandemic, several studies have been published before ours. Perhaps
because of the low baseline suicide rate as well as the rounding of estimates
before and after the pandemic start date, estimates of the pre- and post-pandemic
suicide rates, and thus the change, have varied greatly. We illustrate that
rounding of before and after estimates in one such study, (Bartley et al.,
2020), significantly affects the change estimate as compared to using the
actual estimates. The impact of rounding is much less noticeable when we
analyze the national level data provided by the Centers for Disease
Control and Prevention (CDC). We also illustrate that rounding affects
estimates based on states more than on the national level likely due to the
greater variability in state-level rates. Finally, we illustrate how rounding
can affect inference on the change in poverty rate after the pandemic using
pretend but realistically varying state-level data.

take advantage of small samples of naturally occurring rocks on Earth that have
been deep underground ($\gtrsim 5$ km), accumulating nuclear damage tracks from
recoiling nuclei for $\mathcal{O}(1)$ Gyr. Modern microscopy techniques promise
the capability to read out nuclear damage tracks with nanometer resolution in
macroscopic samples. Thanks to their $\mathcal{O}(1)$ Gyr integration times,
paleo-detectors could constitute nuclear recoil detectors with keV recoil
energy thresholds and 100 kilotonne-yr exposures. This combination would allow
paleo-detectors to probe DM-nucleon cross sections orders of magnitude below
existing upper limits from conventional direct detection experiments. In this
article, we use improved background modeling and a new spectral analysis
technique to update the sensitivity forecast for paleo-detectors. Our results

is data-centric, of
which one fundamental challenge is to understand the influence of data quality
to ML training -- "Which training examples are 'guilty' in making the trained
ML model predictions inaccurate or unfair?" Modeling data influence for ML
training has attracted intensive interest over the last decade, and one popular
framework is to compute the Shapley value of each training example with respect
to utilities such as validation accuracy and fairness of the trained ML model.
Unfortunately, despite recent intensive interest and research, existing methods
only consider a single ML model "in isolation" and do not consider an
end-to-end ML pipeline that consists of data transformations, feature
extractors, and ML training.
  We present DataScope (ease.ml/datascope), the first system that efficiently
computes Shapley values of training examples over an end-to-end ML pipeline,
and illustrate its applications in data debugging for ML training. To this end,
we first develop a novel algorithmic framework that computes Shapley value over
a specific family of ML pipelines that we call canonical pipelines: a positive
relational algebra query followed by a K-nearest-neighbor (KNN) classifier. We
show that, for many subfamilies of canonical pipelines, computing Shapley value
is in PTIME, contrasting the exponential complexity of computing Shapley value
in general. We then put this to practice -- given an sklearn pipeline as input,
DataScope automatically transforms it into an equivalent canonical pipeline, and
efficiently computes Shapley value. We also introduce DataDebugger, a novel
protocol that uses DataScope to debug ML training data via human-in-the-loop
data curation. DataDebugger efficiently computes Shapley value over a canonical
pipeline even when the relational algebra query part of the pipeline is
parameterized. We show that data curation via DataDebugger improves accuracy and
fairness of several ML benchmarks by up to $13\%$ and $5\%$, respectively.
  Summary: (1) We present DataScope, the first system that efficiently computes
Shapley value of training examples over an end-to-end ML pipeline. (2) We
introduce DataDebugger, a novel protocol that uses DataScope to debug ML
training data via human-in-the-loop data curation. (3) We show that data curation
via DataDebugger improves accuracy and fairness of several ML benchmarks by up
to $13\%$ and $5\%$, respectively.

  Federated Learning (FL) is a emerging technique to collaborate the model
training without gathering private data. However, there are still some
limitations, e.g., sample heterogeneity, non-IID distribution, and data
sparsity. Moreover, the intelligent transportation system (ITS) is a complex
system of systems (SoS) consisting of vehicles, roadside units (RRUs), and
infrastructure. The components of ITS are typically different in terms of
computing capabilities, leading to heterogeneous learning challenges in FL. To
address these challenges, we propose a multi-task federated learning framework
for ITS with multi-task learning, heterogeneous learning, and federated
transfer learning. This framework collaboratively trains the network, covert
the learning knowledge to the superordinate network via transfer learning, and
implements the different task-specific networks according to the function
requirements of vehicles and RRUs. Our proposed framework adapts various models
to the different computing capabilities in ITS and leads to accurate and
efficient performance. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated
through various experiments. Moreover, the proposed framework has practical
value for the development of intelligent transportation systems based on FL and
multi-task learning.

number of qubits can be generated in a single operation. This property has many
potential applications, and may specifically be useful for quantum error
correction (QEC). Stabilizer measurements can then be implemented using a
single multi-qubit gate instead of several two-qubit gates, thus reducing
circuit depth. In this study, the toric code is used as a benchmark to compare
the performance of two-qubit and five-qubit gates within parity-check circuits.
We consider trapped ion qubits that are controlled via Raman transitions, where
the primary source of error is assumed to be spontaneous photon scattering. We
show that a five-qubit M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate offers an approximately
$40\%$ improvement over two-qubit gates in terms of the fault tolerance
threshold. This result indicates an advantage of using multi-qubit gates in the
context of QEC.
  We also investigate the logical error per unit time for the toric code
compiled into parity-check circuits using either two-qubit or five-qubit
gates. We find that, for the same level of resource utilization, circuits
constructed with five-qubit gates run approximately $0.5\times$ faster than
circuits made up of two-qubit gates. This result indicates a speedup in the
context of QEC, where an improvement in the logical error rate per unit time
is attained without altering the fault tolerance threshold. The speedout
factor is found to be directly proportional to the square of the number of qubits
in the multi-qubit gate, suggesting a general applicability in this context.
Finally, we discuss the practical implementation of multi-qubit gates within
parity-check circuits, and the use of gate pipelining to minimize overhead.
Our results demonstrate the usefulness of multi-qubit gates within QEC protocols.
We argue that the potential benefits to resource utilization and fault
tolerance make multi-qubit gates worth investigating further in the context of
QEC.

optimization techniques to find the power loading at the source and relay
nodes. Further, an optimization for power loading at relaying nodes along with
relay selection and sub carrier assignment for the fixed power allocation at

address the problem of deriving safe trajectories for CAVs in a mixed traffic
environment that prioritizes rear-end collision avoidance when the preceding

methodologies (pre-training, transfer learning, in-batch augmentation,

question, we perform an extensive experiment on sentiment analysis, machine

English, Chinese, Spanish, German. For sentiment analysis, we find that
back-translation works for many settings but may not be the best choice for
languages with limited translation data. For machine translation, we find that

summarization, we find that copy augmentation is a must-have for all settings.

factors provide one general way to compare different hypotheses by their
compatibility with the observed data. Those quantifications can then also be
used to choose between hypotheses. While Bayes factors provide an immediate
approach to hypothesis testing, they are highly sensitive to details of the
data/model assumptions. Moreover it's not clear how straightforwardly this
approach can be implemented in practice, and in particular how sensitive it is
to the details of the computational implementation. Here, we investigate these
questions for Bayes factor analyses in the cognitive sciences. We explain the
statistics underlying Bayes factors as a product of time-average likelihoods

factors depend on the strength of the evidence as well as the complexity of the

factors will yield the same results; and (3) whether there are strategies to
increase the utility of Bayes factors in the cognitive sciences. Our results
demystify Bayes factors and show that they are inferentially powerful tools,
but depend critically on operational assumptions (e.g., on prior width and
normality, on computational precision and strategy) that can be tailored to

NN-based inference is more complicated than in traditional methods. This is
because in addition to aleatoric uncertainty associated with noisy data, there
is also uncertainty due to limited data, but also due to NN hyperparameters,
overparametrization, optimization and sampling errors as well as model
misspecification. Although there are some recent works on uncertainty
quantification (UQ) in NNs, there is no systematic investigation of suitable
methods towards quantifying the total uncertainty effectively and efficiently
even for function approximation, and there is even less work on solving partial
differential equations and learning operator mappings between
infinite-dimensional function spaces using NNs. In this work, we present a
comprehensive framework that includes uncertainty modeling, new and existing
solution methods, as well as evaluation metrics and post-hoc improvement
approaches. To demonstrate the applicability and reliability of our framework,
we present an extensive comparative study in which various methods are tested
for several exemplary problems (least squares, differential equations,
operator estimation and multi-fidelity learning) with different amounts of
certainty. Based on the results, we draw conclusions on the choice of methods
and their combinations and present a general-purpose learning algorithm that
automatically selects the most suitable UQ method or NN architecture
depending on the problem. The present work represents a crucial step towards
developing practical UQ methods for NNs and will facilitate further
research towards improving uncertainty estimation and solving more complex
problems.

9, Chile, and especially its capital
city, Santiago, suffered from widespread violence with public and private
infrastructure destruction. This work aims to expand an epidemiological
non-local model that successfully described the French riots of 2005 to
incorporate the topology of Santiago's subway network and explain the reported
distribution of rioting activity in the city. Although the model reproduced the
disorders' aggregated temporal evolution, it could not deliver results
resembling the observed spatial distribution of activity on Santiago. The main
reason for this failure can be attributed to the fact that the model lacks a
population displacement mechanism, which seems vital to explain Santiago's
unrest episodes.
  A simplified Santiago network model that only accounts for the city's 31
communes and its non-local interactions did reproduce the observed aggregated
temporal behavior of the riots, but it could not explain the default ranking of
the communes with the highest activity. A more detailed Santiago network, which
includes 106 subway stations as well as 31 communes, and considers non-local
interactions between communes and their nearest subway stations, could also
reproduce the aggregated temporal results but failed to generate the correct
ranking of the communes with the highest activity. Both models consider
one-way trips from communes/stations to the system's origin (mainly home) and
only allow for the transmission of the unrest spirit from the system's origin
to the destination. As Santiago's unrest seemed to be more mobile than what
these conditions imply, further developments of the model will be necessary to
explain the city's experience during the reported disturbances.

effective $3\times 3$ leptonic mixing matrix (LMM) is in general non-unitary.
We revisit the question of what is our current knowledge of individual LMM
matrix elements without assuming unitarity. We define two minimal sets of
experimental constraints -- direct $+$ inherent bounds and indirect bounds, and
analyze the implications of each set on leptonic non-unitarity. In addition, we
clarify the treatment of flux and cross-section predictions, taking into
account NP contamination in hadronic inputs. We use the currently running
FASER$\nu$ experiment as a case study in order to demonstrate the sensitivity
of collider neutrino experiments to leptonic non-unitarity. We find that
indirect bounds constrain LMM non-unitarity to below the $10^{-3}$ level,
stronger than current CKM non-unitarity constraints. Conversely, considering
only direct and inherent bounds we find that ${\cal O}(1)$ unitarity violation
is viable at $2\sigma$, and will be probed by the FASER$\nu$ experiment in the
current run of the LHC.
  Finally, we calculate the future sensitivity of optimal searches for
non-Unitary Leptonic Mixing Matrix (LMM) parameters in the context of
contaminated neutrino interactions at colliders. We demonstrate that even
though indirect bounds are very strong, optimal search strategies for
non-Unitarity in the LMM can yield significant enhancements in sensitivity over
merely looking at individual LMM elements. We find that future collider
experiments can reach values of $|u_\ell u^\dagger_{\ell'}|^2\sim 10^{-5}$ with
only $0.1\,{\rm ab}^{-1}$ of cumulative integrated luminosity.
  In addition, we present a general method for computing the sensitivity of
searches for the product of two complex quantities, which can be applied to a
variety of beyond-the-Standard-Model scenarios.

and complement operators and consider regular expressions on infinite alphabets
based on potentially infinite character sets. Standard approaches deciding the

  We give a new symbolic decision procedure for the containment problem based
on Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting
approach to check containment. We generalize Brzozowski's syntactic derivative
operator to two derivative operators that work with respect to (potentially
infinite) representable character sets.
  The algorithm avoids the translation to an expresson-equivalent automaton and
provides a purely symbolic term rewriting systems for solving regular expressions
inequalities.
  We prove that the algorithm is sound and complete, and it is significantly
more efficient than the standard approaches, as it does not involve any
translation to an automaton and the size of the rewriting systems is, in
practice, always finite.
  We implemented our algorithm in a prototype tool called Derivatives and proved
its effectiveness by deciding a large set of regular expression inequalities
extracted from the standard library of the Racket programming language and the
standard problem library of the Agda proof assistant.

containment problem in the Agda proof assistant and prove some important
properties of regular expressions inequalities in the meta-theory of Agda.

benchmarked on inequalities from the standard problem library and its results
confirm the high efficiency of the algorithm.

programmable network using regular expressions by translating network
specifications to regular expressions and using regular expressions inequalities
to represent and prove network properties.

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms exploit the information from camera
and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation. Recent deep learning
based VIO models attract attentions as they provide pose information in a
data-driven way, without the need of designing hand-crafted algorithms.
Existing learning based VIO models rely on recurrent models to fuse multimodal
data and process sensor signal, which are hard to train and not efficient
enough. We propose a novel learning based VIO framework with external memory
attention that effectively and efficiently combines visual and inertial
features for states estimation. Our proposed model is able to estimate pose
accurately and robustly, even in challenging scenarios, e.g., over-ground
navigation and underwater navigation. Compared with traditional VIO algorithms
and existing learning based VIO models, our proposed model is able to produce
smooth states estimates and outperform them in terms of accuracy. The code
and data are available online: \url{https://github.com/Shu-ZhangUMD/VIOMem}.
  The code is implemented by PyTorch and we use Pytorch-Lightweight-GNN to train
our VIO model. We appreciate the authors of DeepVO, LIVONet, and FVO for

also thank Bonsignour et al. \cite{bonsignour2020visual} and Brescio et al.

  The study of parafermion algebras for simple affine Lie superalgebras started
about thirty years ago, when it was initiated by Kac and Wakimoto for
$osp(1|2)$. Since 2008, Lei and Zhang have studied this subject for
$osp(m|2n)$. Our choice of generators is inspired by the $osp(1|2)$ case and
its connection to the Trigonometric Ruijsenaars-Schneider model. In contrast to
the $osp(1|2)$ case, the study for $osp(1|2n), n>1$ is more complicated
because the pseudo-vectors $h_{\pm}\nu_{j}$ is not nilpotent, so the
negative power of $\nu_{j}$ is involved in the study. We observe that the
study of this kind of algebras shares similarities with the study of the
Fock-Araki-Haag algebra in QFT.
  Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a simple affine superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, and
$\mathfrak{b}$ a Borel subalgebra of the finite part of $\mathfrak{g}$. The
structure of the parafermion algebra attached to an integrable highest weight
module for $(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{b})$ is similar to that of the
Bozejowska-Mirgowski superalgebra associated with the pair
$(\mathfrak{sl}(1|2n),\mathfrak{sl}(1|2))$. The generators of this algebra are
similar to those of the Gelfand-Dynkin algebra associated with
$\mathfrak{sl}(1|2n)$. These generators are subject to the same quadratic
relations as those of the Gelfand-Dynkin algebra, with the additional relations
generated by the even part of $\mathfrak{b}$. Our choice of the set of
generators is inspired by the study of the superalgebra $osp(1|2)$ and its
connection to the Trigonometric Ruijsenaars-Schneider model.

knowledge-amalgamation problem, termed
Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA). The goal of FedSA is to train a
student model for a new task with the help of several decentralized teachers,
whose pre-training tasks and data are different and agnostic. Our motivation
for investigating such a problem setup stems from a recent dilemma of model
sharing. Many researchers or institutes have spent enormous resources on
training large and competent networks. Due to the privacy, security, or
intellectual property issues, they are, however, not able to share their own
pre-trained models, even if they wish to contribute to the community. The
proposed FedSA offers a solution to this dilemma and makes it one step further
since, again, the learned student may specialize in a new task different from
all of the teachers. To this end, we proposed a dedicated strategy for handling
FedSA. Specifically, our student-training process is driven by a novel
saliency-based approach that adaptively selects teachers as the participants
and integrates their representative capabilities into the student. To evaluate
the effectiveness of FedSA, we conduct experiments on both single-task and
multi-task settings. Experimental results demonstrate that FedSA effectively
amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models and achieves competitive
performance to centralized baselines.

the rotation of solar-type stars goes
through different phases: a rapid spin-down during the first gigayear, a possible
slowing down until the break age of about 2.6 Gyr, and finally a rapid spin-up
until the birth mass cut-off of neutron stars and black holes. The previous
slowing down phase is supported by indirect arguments and global stellar
evolution models, but there is currently no direct observational evidence. In
this work, we use the rotation-activity relation for old solar-type stars
excluded by global models from the main sequencing phase of spin-down to
re-evaluate the long-term spin evolution. Using the Rossby number defined by
Georgiev et al. (2017), we show that all stars excluded by global models
populate a scaling law consistent with a simple power-law equation of state
describing the slowing down: $\mbox{Ro} \propto P_{\rm rot}^2$. This scaling
law is also consistent with global models for short rotation periods. We
construct a new rotational model compatible with the observed scaling law for
long rotation periods and show that it is self-consistent with the fundamental
physical assumptions of global models. The new model indicates that the angular
momentum loss rate decreases weakly with decreasing rotation for most evolutionary
states of solar-type stars. This works in the same direction as the revised
rotation-convection argument of Spada et al. (2013) and explains the sharp
cutoff in the rotation-activity relation for slow rotators. The new model also
predicts a population of dormant active stars, which could explain some
persistent ultra-high energy cosmic rays. Finally, the new model changes the
expected age spread in populations of dormant or dormant-like active stars from
a few hundred Myr to more than 4 Gyr.
  We discuss the observational signatures that could constrain the rotational
evolution models, in particular the expected population of dormant active stars
and the broad activity-rotation relation could be used to constrain the age
spread in the case of young (e.g., less than a Gyr) star samples. We show that
the non-linear relation between activity and rotation strongly modifies the
interpretation of the activity-age relations constructed by several authors and
may explain their slope variations. Finally, we argue that the sample selection
effects, previously discussed by us and others, is also powered by a population
spread in the activity-rotation relation.

the atmosphere of Venus, and
modulation of its composition by interior-exterior cycling. The formation and
evolution of Venus's atmosphere, leading to contemporary surface conditions,
remain hotly debated topics, and involve questions that tie into many
disciplines. We explore these various inter-related mechanisms which shaped the
evolution of the atmosphere, starting with the volatile sources and sinks.
Going from the deep interior to the top of the atmosphere, we describe volcanic
outgassing, surface atmosphere interactions, and atmosphere escape.
Furthermore, we address more complex aspects of the history of Venus, including
the role of Late Accretion impacts, how magnetic field generation is tied into
long-term evolution, and the implications of geochemical and geodynamical
feedback cycles for atmospheric evolution. We highlight plausible end-member
evolutionary pathways that Venus could have followed, from accretion to its
present-day state, based on modeling and observations. In a first scenario, the
planet was desiccated by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase. In a
second scenario, Venus could have harbored surface liquid water for long
periods of time, until its temperate climate was destabilized and it entered a
runaway greenhouse phase. In a third scenario, Venus's inefficient outgassing
could have kept water inside the planet, where hydrogen was trapped in the core
and the mantle was oxidized. We discuss these scenarios in the context of
astrobiological interest in Venus and its possible habitability in the past or
present. Testing these scenarios will require continued observations from
orbit and from the surface of Venus when missions allow for prolonged
operations. Such investigations will aid our understanding of atmospheric
evolution and its connections to interior-source cycling on Venus.

desiccation factor" ($DF$), which characterizes the degree of desiccation of a

of laser-induced
surface chemistry. Chemical reactions on the surface of charged droplets are
ubiquitous in nature and can provide critical insight into more efficient
processes for industrial chemical production. Here, we demonstrate the
application of the reaction nanoscopy technique to strong-field ionized
nanodroplets of propanediol (PDO). The technique's sensitivity to the
near-field around the droplet allows for the in-situ characterization of the
average droplet size and charge. The use of ultrashort laser pulses enables
control of the amount of surface charge by the laser intensity. Moreover, we
demonstrate the surface chemical sensitivity of reaction nanoscopy by comparing
droplets of the isomers 1,2-PDO and 1,3-PDO in their ion emission and
fragmentation channels. Referencing the ion yields to gas-phase data, we find
an enhanced production of methyl cations from droplets of the 1,2-PDO isomer.
Density functional theory simulations support that this enhancement is due to
the alignment of 1,2-PDO molecules on the surface. The results pave the way
towards spatio-temporal observations of charge dynamics and surface reactions
on droplets in pump-probe studies.
  We also investigate the effect of the droplet size on the ion yields of
droplets of the 1,2-PDO isomer. Below a critical size (approximately 120 nm)
the ion yields are independent of the droplet size whereas for larger droplets
the ion yields increase with decreasing droplet size. This behavior is
consistent with the surface chemistry being controlled by the electrical
field strength in the ionization plasma around the droplet.
  Finally, we study the effect of the droplet charge on the ion yields. With
increasing charge the ion yields either increase with the charge (for large
charges) or decrease with the charge (for low charges). This behavior is
consistent with the surface chemistry being controlled by the electrical
field strength in the ionization plasma around the droplet.
  The results open up new perspectives for the optimization of chemical
processes from droplets and the investigation of charge and particle dynamics
in general.

"quantum-inspired" nature of TNs permits them to be mapped to parametrized
quantum circuits (PQCs), a fact which has inspired recent proposals for
enhancing the performance of TN algorithms using near-term quantum devices, as
well as enabling joint quantum-classical training frameworks which benefit from
the distinct strengths of TN and PQC models. However, the success of any such
methods depends on efficient and accurate methods for approximating TN states
using realistic quantum circuits, something which remains an unresolved
question. In this work, we compare a range of novel and previously-developed
algorithmic protocols for decomposing matrix product states (MPS) of arbitrary
bond dimensions into low-depth quantum circuits consisting of stacked linear
layers of two-qubit unitaries. These protocols are formed from different
combinations of a preexisting analytical decomposition scheme with constrained
optimization of circuit unitaries, and all possess efficient classical
runtimes. Our experimental results reveal one particular protocol, involving
sequential growth and optimization of the quantum circuit, to outperform all
other methods, with even greater benefits seen in the setting of limited
computational resources. Given these promising results, we believe this protocol
to be a strong candidate for use in any future TN-to-PQC mapping algorithm, and
to help to deliver the greatest practice benefits for enhancing TN performance
using near-term quantum devices, as well as for exploring novel TN-PQC
hybrid models for machine learning and other applications.

second promising protocol, which is less successful in practice, can be

from quantum information theory and optimization. This suggests to us that there
may be a gap between the theoretical guarantees of analysis-based protocols,
which can be proved correct but are now outdated in terms of performance, and
the superior but generally uncertain performance of learning-based protocols.

  Let M be a combinatorial differential manifold. To each vertex v of M we
associate a lookup table Lv that encodes the differential information
associated to v. We prove that the Pontrjagin classes of M are precisely the
total classes of the Lv's.

M, and how this ties in with the classification theorem for combinatorial
differential manifolds.

result which generalizes a related discussion by Gelfand and MacPherson on
the classical Pontrjagin classes.

the importance of the lookup tables Lv in the computation of the Pontrjagin
classes of a differential manifold.

differential manifold a "differential label" Lv(v). While this is conceptually
similar to our lookup table Lv(v), it seems to us that our terminology is more
accurate and transparent. Indeed, Lv(v) is precisely that - a lookup table -
containing all the differential information associated to the vertex v, while

the simplices containing v.

approaches. We believe that our framework would provide a transparent
interpretation of the relations between the Pv's and the differential labels
