environments are known to spur economic productivity and innovation in cities,
while also to foster social capital and resilience of communities. However,
mobility restrictions during the pandemic have forced people to substantially
reduce urban physical encounters, raising questions on the social implications
of such behavioral changes. In this paper, we study how the income diversity of
urban encounters have changed during different periods throughout the pandemic,
using a large-scale, privacy-enhanced mobility dataset of more than one million
anonymized mobile phone users in four large US cities, collected across three
years spanning before and during the pandemic. We find that the diversity of
urban encounters have substantially decreased (by 15% to 30%) during the
pandemic and has persisted through late 2021, even though aggregated mobility
metrics have recovered to pre-pandemic levels. Counterfactual analyses show
that while the reduction of outside activities (higher rates of staying at
home) was a major factor that contributed to decreased diversity in the early
stages of the pandemic, behavioral changes including lower willingness to
explore new places and changes in visitation preferences further worsened the
long-term diversity of encounters. Our findings suggest that the pandemic could
have long-lasting negative effects on urban income diversity, and provide
implications for managing the trade-off between the stringency of COVID-19
policies and the diversity of urban encounters as we move beyond the pandemic.
  We make three methodological contributions. First, we develop a metric, "even
ness" (inspired from information theory), to quantify how concentrated
encounters are around the mean income. This metric is easy to understand and
interpret, and provides a comprehensive picture of the degree of income
diversity (or lack thereof) of encounters. Second, we use evenness metric to
examine how the degree of income diversity of encounters has changed across
different years, which allows us to compare the pre-pandemic and pandemic
periods directly within the same population. Third, we use formal statistical
methods to isolate the factors that are most likely to be responsible for the
changes in evenness metric observed across different years, which helps to
attribute specific contributions of changes in behavior to the overall change
in evenness.
  Our key variables are evenness metric $e$ and counterfactual evenness
counterfactual $e_{CF}$. The informal interpretation of $e$ and $e_{CF}$ are
described in the main text.

benchmark. Moreover, the numerical approach to find the feasible secure decoding

than the binary orbital period (typically within a few percent). The
asynchronous polars have been disproportionately detected in soft gamma-ray
observations, leading us to consider the possibility that they have

status and its spectral shape. Using the entire sample of asynchronous polars,

sensitively detect the very weak local magnetic field, which is expelled by the
superconductor (as the "testing magnet") due to the Meissner effect. The

acceleration of the atomic motion in the interferometry and thus can be

atoms have been measured at the accuracy of $10^{-12}$ g, the measured

magnetic material, and the measured sensitivity could reach $10^{-14}$ T as
well. Our proposal offers a new path to measure the expel local field near the
superconductor, and may also be used to measure the magnetic field of a
magnetic material. It can also bridge the quantum world (superconductor) to
the classical world (atomic interferometry).

incorporate the atomic interferometry, and thus develop a new kinetic theory
description for the superconductor by incorporating the atomic interferometry.

linearized Gross-Pitaevskii equation, which might offer new insights on the
superconductor using the atomic interferometry.

may also bridge the quantum world (superconductor) to the classical world (atomic interferometry). It is interesting and worth continuing our investigations.

SIMD high-performance computing, despite the fact that many important HPC
applications have an inherent object structure. On SIMD accelerators, including

  We discovered a broad class of object-oriented programs with many important
real-world applications that can be implemented efficiently on massively
parallel SIMD accelerators. We call this class Single-Method Multiple-Objects
(SMMO), because parallelism is expressed by running a method on all objects of
a type.
  To make fast GPU programming available to average programmers, we developed
DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework for SMMO applications. DynaSOAr consists of (1) a
fully-parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator, (2) a data layout DSL and
(3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. DynaSOAr achieves performance
superior to state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by controlling both memory
allocation and memory access.
  DynaSOAr improves the usage of allocated memory with a Structure of Arrays
data layout and achieves low memory fragmentation through efficient management
of free and allocated memory blocks with lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps.
Contrary to other allocators, DynaSOAr achieves high parallel performance by
ensuring data and instructions are coalesced into warp-sized threads and
instructions, and by providing a highly parallel do-all operation. It is also
one to two orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art memory
allocators POFOA and TBB's memory allocator when accessed sequentially.
  We evaluate DynaSOAr's performance on various benchmarks and algorithms, and
show how it can be combined with other high-performance GPU libraries to
solve various problems, including scientific computing applications, graph
algorithms and computer vision algorithms.
  Finally, we evaluate a C++11 parallel implementation of the QuickSort
algorithm, which illustrates that even generic parallel algorithms can be
very efficient when accessed in a way that minimizes memory alignment problems
and cache misses.
  In summary, DynaSOAr is a highly-performance memory allocator that enables
efficient GPU implementations of SMMO applications and serves as a foundation for
high-performance GPU programming.

Indeed, being based on 1D radiative transfer (RT) theory, they work well only
for horizontally homogeneous clouds. A promising approach for treating clouds
as fully 3D objects is cloud tomography, and this has been demonstrated for
airborne observations. For cloud tomography from space, however, more efficient
forward 3D RT solvers are required. Here, we present a path forward,
acknowledging that optically thick clouds have "veiled cores." Photons
scattered into a certain angle range ($\pi$ sr) do not contribute to the
side lobes in the 1D projection, resulting in the "veil" effect, which
significantly reduces the upscattering and the reconstruction accuracy in
cloud tomography. To quantify this effect, we use a suite of metrics involving
the photon probability distribution function (pdf), the upscattered radiant
flux, and the reconstructed optical thickness and effective particle size. We
then investigate the performance of two 3D RT solvers, SUITE and LIBRT, and
find that, beyond efficiency differences, both solvers can produce projections
with significant veils (metrics variations $>$ 30 %) for optical thickness
greater than approximately 4 and effective particle size greater than
approximately 50 $\mu$m for a convective cloud. This limit translates to a
cloud water content (CWC) of approximately 0.5 g/m$^3$. Below this CWC, veils
produce side lobes in the projections, but up to CWCs of approximately 2
g/m$^3$, veils do not contaminate the core of the cloud. For practical
retrieval purposes, we find that clouds with veils should not be assumed to be
homogeneous, while clouds without veils can be considered homogeneous. A
homogeneity indicator, based on the pdf, is proposed to distinguish these two
classes of clouds. We also propose a 1D adjustment to the 3D projections to
better agree with current 1D retrievals and thus enable homogeneous retrievals
for clouds without veils. Finally, we suggest retrieving the 3D cloud structure
in terms of a probability field, rather than a discrete classification of
clouds as uniform or non-uniform.

Accurate mapping of turbulence using X-ray emission lines is challenging due to

spectral resolution to quantitatively investigate the ICM turbulence at all
scales. Powerful diagnostics for these studies are line shift and the line
broadening maps, and the second-order structure function. When estimating these
quantities, instruments will be limited by uncertainties of their measurements,
and by the sample variance (aka cosmic variance) of the observation. We extend
here the formalism started in our companion paper I to include the effect of
statistical uncertainties in the estimation of these line diagnostics, and to
derive expressions for these uncertainties in the linear regime of structure
functions. We apply this framework to the X-IFU, and to a hypothetical
infrared integral field unit suitable for galaxy clusters observations. We show
that even with idealised sampling (no systematic errors), the cosmic variance
will be a major limitation for the estimation of these line diagnostics when
probing the smallest scales of interest for turbulence in galaxy clusters. We
also show that the statistical uncertainties are crucial to predict sampling
variances, as they strongly affect the number density of points and the
dispersion of the measurements. Finally, we estimate that increasing the
spectroscopic exposure by a factor 10 should yield estimates of line

cluster centre.

that can be analysed. Furthermore, unlike what is commonly done, we do not
conclude that volume-averaging over larger regions will always be an optimal
strategy to mitigate the effect of cosmic variance, as it will also increase

error channel and a generalized Pauli channel decoherence channel for both
qubits and qutrits. For the same error in determination of the mass, the qutrit
simulations can tolerate 10 to 100x larger gate noise than a qubit simulations.

future with a qutrits but is infeasible using qubits.

qutrits also have a ~16x greater tolerance to amplitude damping than the qubits
and a ~8x greater tolerance to the generalized Pauli channel decay.

the same level of accuracy.

qubits before critical failure due to decoherence.

broader class of systems.

quantum simulations should first benchmark their protocol against a qutrit
model to gauge the level of technical proficiency.

approaches for correlating the arrival directions of neutrinos with the arrival
directions of UHECRs. The neutrino data is provided by the IceCube Neutrino

is provided by the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array. All
experiments provide increased statistics and improved reconstructions with
respect to our previous results reported in 2015. The first analysis uses a
high-statistics neutrino sample optimized for point-source searches to search
for excesses of neutrinos clustering in the vicinity of UHECR directions. The
second analysis searches for an excess of UHECRs in the direction of the
highest-energy neutrinos. The third analysis searches for an excess of pairs of
UHECRs and highest-energy neutrinos on different angular scales. None of the
analyses has found a significant excess, and previously reported
over-fluctuations are reduced in significance. Based on these results, we
update the confidence levels for the hypothesis that the UHECRs are of primary
proton/photon origin and that the neutrinos are extra Galactic to $>$0.06 (0.03)
for all three analyses, respectively.

neutrinos from the interaction of UHECR nuclei with the cosmic microwave
background before publishing the nuclear data. The search uses a new data
analysis with improved reconstructions and selection criteria as well as an
updated neutrino analysis with a new sample of high-energy astrophysical
muon neutrinos. An excess of neutrinos with energies $\geq$400 GeV in a 2$^\circ$
radius around UHECR heavy nucleus directions is observed with a significance of
3.2$\sigma$. The excess is most prominent for the most energetic nuclei. The
final analysis results are consistent with the hypothesis that the neutrino
excess is caused by the interaction of UHECR nuclei with the cosmic microwave
background before the primary collisions.

nonequilibrium thermodynamics to study expansion/contraction processes. Here,
the numbers of initial and final microstates are different so they cannot be
connected by unique Hamiltonian trajectories. This commonly happens when the

trajectories that can be inverted to yield an identity mapping between initial
and final microstates as the parameter in the Hamiltonian is changed. We
propose a trick to overcome this hurdle with a focus on free expansion in an
isolated system, where the concept of dissipated work is not clear. The trick
is shown to be thermodynamically consistent and can be extremely useful in
simulation. We justify that it is the thermodynamic average of the internal
microwork done by a microstate that is dissipated; this microwork is different
from the exchange microwork with the vacuum, which vanishes. We also establish
that the microwork is nonnegative for free expansion, which is remarkable,
since its sign is not fixed in a general process.

simulating free expansion in small quantum systems. Nonequilibrium
thermodynamics is well known to fail for the Loschmidt state, which has
full quantum entanglement among all particles. We propose a trick to simulate
it by placing an effective barrier that splits the system into two subsystems.
The trick is thermodynamically consistent and consistent with the expectation
that the Loschmidt state cannot be reached by any quench. We also study two
mixtures of Bose-Einstein condensates with different temperatures and densities
that are now becoming experimentally realistic. The microwork concept is
particularly useful in these nonequilibrium scenarios where the usual
coarse-grained work is not adequate.

quantum systems, which can be extremely useful in simulation, and is
thermodynamically consistent. We demonstrate its consistency for several
scenarios, and emphasize that it is the thermodynamic average of the internal
microwork that is dissipated; this microwork is different from the exchange
microwork with the vacuum, which vanishes.

  This article describes our type-based static verification tool HELMHOLTZ for
Michelson, which is a statically typed stack-based language for writing smart
contracts that are executed on the blockchain platform Tezos. HELMHOLTZ is
designed on top of our extension of Michelson's type system with refinement
types. HELMHOLTZ takes a Michelson program annotated with a user-defined
specification written in the form of a refinement type as input; it then
typechecks the program against the specification based on the refinement type
system, discharging the generated verification conditions with the SMT solver
Z3. We briefly introduce our refinement type system for the core calculus
Mini-Michelson of Michelson, which incorporates the characteristic features
such as compound datatypes (e.g., lists and pairs), higher-order functions, and
invocation of another contract. \HELMHOLTZ{} successfully verifies several
practical Michelson programs, including one that transfers money to an account
and that checks a digital signature.
  Furthermore, we present our approach to verifiably implementing a
\textit{contract}, that is, a sequence of smart contracts automating
transactions between several parties. Our approach is based on a two-stage
verification process: first, we verify that each transition between two
contracts indeed performs the intended transaction; then HELMHOLTZ checks that
the drop-out of each contract satisfies the requirements of the transition,
together with a further condition specified by each owner of the account. We
also demonstrate a verifiably implemented contract that transfers money from one
account to another via a temporary account.
  HELMHOLTZ nicely shows the strengths of the refinement type system, which
ensures correctness of a program at compile time and eliminates the need for
reverse engineering to extract specifications from existing programs. It also
delivers novel features of Michelson such as compound datatypes and higher-order
functions, which are essential for writing efficient smart contracts. Finally,
HELMHOLTZ provides a generic way of defining specifications for transfer
transactions, which is crucial for ensuring the correctness of contracts that

) and imperative algorithms
(pseudocodes) are two well-known coexisting concepts. Then what is their
relationship? Our answer is that
  \[ imperative\ algorithms\ =\ proofs\ with\ cuts \]
  This observation leads to a generalization to pseudocodes which we call {\it
logical pseudocodes}. It is similar to natural deduction proof of computability
logic\cite{Jap03,Jap08}. Each statement in it corresponds to a proof step in
natural deduction. Therefore, the merit over pseudocode is that each statement
is guaranteed to be correct and safe with respect to the initial
specifications. It can also be seen as an extension to computability logic web
(\colw) with forward reasoning capability.
  We demonstrate its power and usefulness by two developments of protocols
design for authentication in distributed systems. They are easier and more
intuitive than the counterparts in \colw. They also cover some mistakes that
one should avoid when designing such protocols in distributed systems. The
logical pseudocodes are independent of the underlying communication model of
\colw. Therefore, they can be implemented over various communication protocols
including those defined in \colw.
  All observations and investigations in this paper are implemented in our
protocol design tool called $\mathcal{CO}L$~assistant\cite{CoLassistant}. The
tool is also developed to help developing and testing protocols based on the
logical pseudocodes. It reports on any incorrect or unsafe statements in the
pseudocodes if they are not guaranteed to terminate or lead to the desired
specifications. It then helps to fix them automatically. The development of
protocols in the tool is simpler, easier, and more intuitive than implementing
them directly in pseudocode without the tool. This is because the logical
pseudocodes for specifying and developing protocols are more intuitive and
integrated with the proof system of computability logic which guarantees
correctness and safety of the specifications.
  Finally, the logical pseudocodes open up new avenues for proof-based
specifications and implementations of distributed protocols. It also provides
another perspective on the advantage of proof-based approaches over
test-based ones when developing distributed protocols.

robotics. We present a study on using learning-based methods for solving this
problem online from a single RGB image, whilst training our models with
entirely synthetic data. We study three main approaches: one direct regression
model that directly predicts the extrinsic matrix from an image, one sparse
correspondence model that regresses 2D keypoints and then uses PnP, and one
dense correspondence model that uses regressed depth and segmentation maps to
enable ICP pose estimation. In our experiments, we benchmark these methods
against each other and against well-established classical methods, to find the
surprising result that direct regression outperforms other approaches, and we
perform noise-sensitivity analysis to gain further insights into these results.

eye-in-hand camera calibration, with no need for sparse or dense correspondence.
This is a rare conclusion in the learning-on-visual-task literature, which we
attribute to the strong ability of modern neural networks to model imaging
variability, and also to the simplicity and robustness of least-squares optimisation.

an image from incomplete and/or
degraded measurements. Such problems arise in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI),
computed tomography, deblurring, superresolution, inpainting, and other
applications. It is often the case that many image hypotheses are consistent
with both the measurements and prior information, and so the goal is not to
recover a single "best" hypothesis but rather to explore the space of probable
hypotheses, i.e., to sample from the posterior distribution. In this work, we
propose a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN that can generate dozens of
high-quality posterior samples per second. Using quantitative evaluation
metrics like conditional Fr\'{e}chet inception distance, we demonstrate that
our method produces state-of-the-art posterior samples in both multicoil MRI
and inpainting applications.
  By incorporating Kullback-Liebler divergence-regularized adversarial training
with a conditional discriminator, we are able to produce realistic posterior
samples in these inverse problems. Perhaps surprisingly, we find that the
conditional discriminator need only see a small set of simple synthetic
images to learn to distinguish posterior samples from our generator and a
corresponding set of real samples. We use our generator to produce multiple
state-of-the-art solutions to the problem of MRI reconstruction from very

scattering screens, most of
unknown origin. Scintillation studies of pulsars provides a sensitive tool for
resolving these scattering screens and a means of measuring their properties.
In this paper, we report our analysis of 34 years of Arecibo observations of
PSR B1133+16, from which we have obtained high-quality dynamic spectra and
their associated scintillation arcs, arising from the scattering screens
located along the line of sight to the pulsar. We have identified six
individual scattering screens that are responsible for the observed
scintillation arcs, which persist for decades. Using the assumption that the
scattering screens have not changed significantly in this time, we have modeled
the variations in arc curvature throughout the Earth's orbit and extracted
information about the placement, orientation, and velocity of five of the six
screens, which agree well with previous studies. Moreover, this analysis has
laid bare a new sixth screen, previously undetected, which has a very small
value of $|b|\lesssim 10$ pc and has changed significantly since the start of
the observations. We estimate that this screen is likely to be a massive,
progenitor star. Further analysis of more pulsar observations is required to
fully exploit the power of scintillation arcs to resolve the interstellar
medium and will help to identify the sources of newly discovered scattering
screens.
  We also report the identification of two extragalactic scattering screens
along the line of sight to PSR B1032+10 and PSR B0031-07, using their
scintillation arcs in combination with the arcs from the pulsar itself. These
screens are likely to be the scattering regions near the active galactic
nucleus (AGN) J0303+0255 and AGN J0237+0057 discovered towards these pulsars,
which are now found to be 1.14 $\pm$ 0.12 kpc and 0.74 $\pm$ 0.09 kpc away,
respectively, as determined from the velocities of the arcs. These values
agree well with extinction measurements towards these pulsars and previous
single-component scattering studies of these pulsars.
  Finally, we report the failure to identify any additional scattering screens
along the lines of sight to the pulsar pairs PSR B0031-07/PSR B0031-07 and
PSR B1133+16/PSR B1133+

controllability of vanilla WaveNet (WN) using pitch-dependent dilated
convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). Specifically, as a probabilistic
autoregressive generation model with stacked dilated convolution layers, WN
achieves high-fidelity audio waveform generation. However, the pure-data-driven
nature and the lack of prior knowledge of audio signals degrade the pitch
controllability of WN. For instance, it is difficult for WN to precisely
generate the periodic components of audio signals when the given auxiliary
fundamental frequency ($F_{0}$) features are outside the $F_{0}$ range observed
in the training data. To address this problem, QPNet with two novel designs is
proposed. First, the PDCNN component is applied to dynamically change the
network architecture of WN according to the given auxiliary $F_{0}$ features.
Second, a cascaded network structure is utilized to simultaneously model the
long- and short-term dependencies of quasi-periodic signals such as speech. The
performances of single-tone sinusoid and speech generations are evaluated. The
experimental results show the effectiveness of the PDCNNs for unseen auxiliary
$F_{0}$ features and the effectiveness of the cascaded structure for speech
generation.

of translating speech in one language
into text in another language. Traditional cascaded approaches for ST, using
Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) systems, are
prone to error propagation. End-to-end approaches use only one system to avoid
propagating error, yet are difficult to employ due to data scarcity. We explore
zero-shot translation, which enables translating a pair of languages that is
unseen during training, thus avoid the use of end-to-end ST data. Zero-shot
translation has been shown to work for multilingual machine translation, yet
has not been studied for speech translation. We attempt to build zero-shot ST
models that are trained only on ASR and MT tasks but can do ST task during
inference. The challenge is that the representation of text and audio is
significantly different, thus the models learn ASR and MT tasks in different
ways, making it non-trivial to perform zero-shot. These models tend to output
the wrong language when performing zero-shot ST. We tackle the issues by
including additional training data and an auxiliary loss function that
minimizes the text-audio difference. Our experiment results and analysis show
that the methods are promising for zero-shot ST. Moreover, our methods are
particularly useful in the few-shot settings where a limited amount of ST data
is available, with improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU scores over the baseline
that uses only few-shot data.

non-geometric in nature. To better understand this intersection product, we
study three Landau-Ginzburg models: the original one of Tseng-You, a
variation due to Fan-Wu-You, and the Landau-Ginzburg model associated to the
irreducible representation of $\mathbb{C}^* \times \mathbb{C}^*$. We show that
the Fan-Wu-You variation is better suited to compute relative $I$-functions. We
also conjecture that its algebra of observables is isomorphic to the algebra of
relative quantum cohomology.
  Finally, we propose a conjecture that connects our study of variations of
relative quantum cohomology to Yangians. Its connection formula recalls that of
Frenkel-Hernandez but its presentation is simpler and more explicit. It
unifies the study of regular and irregular connections, quantum cohomology and
FJRW theory. We also propose conjectures that connect our variation of
relative quantum cohomology to Beilinson-Drinfeld correspondence and to
Crystals.
  As an appendix, we have included a survey of regular and irregular
connections through the lens of relative quantum cohomology.

vectorial data. ViDaExpert is able to work with data tables of "object-feature"
type that might contain numerical feature values as well as textual labels for
rows (objects) and columns (features). ViDaExpert implements several
statistical methods such as standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis
(PCA) and the method of elastic maps (non-linear version of PCA), Linear
Discriminant Analysis (LDA), multilinear regression, K-Means clustering, a
variant of decision tree construction algorithm. Equipped with several
user-friendly dialogs for configuring data point representations (size, shape,
color) and fast 3D viewer, ViDaExpert is a handy tool allowing to construct an
interactive 3D-scene representing a table of data in multidimensional space and
perform its quick and insightfull statistical analysis, from basic to advanced
methods.
  The source code is distributed under LGPL license and is developed using
MS-Visual Studio.Net framework. It contains some MS-VBA macros for
integration with Microsoft Office Excel, which is default choice for data
analysis and processing in ViDaExpert. You may import your Excel spreadsheets
into ViDaExpert using ViBaImport macro or ViBaLink component or simply copy/paste
the data from Excel into ViDaExpert's data table. ViDaExpert is designed to
work with medium-sized data tables (up to few millions data points) and is a
practical tool for Data Mining applications.
  ViDaExpert is developed by Vladimir G. Shpall, PhD in Mathematical Physics,
and is his personal contribution to the open source community. If you have any
ideas how to improve it or you need help with data analysis - feel free to
contact the author via e-mail: vshpall(at)mail.ru
  ViDaExpert contains the following main modules:
  - ViDaExplorer - main program representing a table of data in 3D-space,
    performing interactive rotations and selections of data points,
    displaying statistical information about the data table and its subsets.
  - ViDaStat - program for fast statistical analysis of a data table,
    implementing various well-known algorithms (PCA, LDA, K-Means, decision
    tree construction), it can also be called from ViDaExplorer for each data
    table or from the command line for batch processing.
  - ViBaImport - Excel VBA macro allowing to import data tables from MS-Office
    Excel

Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complicated domains typically
require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we present a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction computations over an unstructured mesh becomes
roughly the same as the time cost of the FMM-based far field interaction
computation. One of the key components of our algorithm is the high-order 2-D
monomial approximation of a function over a mesh element, which is often
regarded as an ill-conditioned problem, since it involves the solution of a
Vandermonde linear system. In fact, it has long been observed that, when the
function is sufficiently smooth, and when a backward stable linear system
solver is used, the resulting monomial expansion can approximate the function
uniformly to high accuracy. We rigorously formalize this observation in this
paper. The performance of our algorithm is illustrated through several
numerical experiments.
